candidates.name: KOC-LNS: key-ordered coalition LNS with plan max-consensus
candidates.one_line: A decentralized, deadlock-free LNS for heterogeneous coalition scheduling. Each robot runs its own anytime search, and the robots agree through loss-tolerant plan-level max-consensus. It targets the public HeteroMRTA (RA-L 2025) and Sadcher (MRS 2025) test sets. In a pilot, a 4 s single-core centralized version already has 13.4% lower makespan than the published RL SOTA and matches the MILP level.
candidates.arena: PRIMARY: the HeteroMRTA test families (Dai et al., IEEE RA-L 10(3) 2025; code github.com/marmotlab/HeteroMRTA, Apache-2.0, with a released checkpoint). This covers the shipped RALTestSet (50 instances, 15 agents in 5 species, 20 tasks) plus regenerated 50-instance sets for all 13 published SA-BT, SA-AT and MA-AT configurations (kn 9-50, km 20-50), built with the repo generator and fixed seeds. Metrics: mean makespan, success rate, average waiting time and wall-clock at a matched compute budget, plus percent gap to an exact MILP where one solves. SECONDARY: the Sadcher MRTA-250K test split (CC BY 4.0, data.4tu.nl/datasets/10e28ee0-9ad9-450d-8be7-6e6a91f2931f; 8 tasks x 3 robots with MILP-optimal labels; metric is gap to optimum) and Sadcher's scaling protocol (3, 5 and 20 robots, up to 250 tasks, with precedence). TERTIARY, prespecified and labelled self-defined: the same instances under Gilbert-Elliott loss of 0-70%, partitions and execution noise, to show what decentralization buys. ARENA WEIGHING (why this arena and not the others): (1) LoRR scheduling. Parsing the 2024 Code-Archive leaderboard shows that even a per-instance portfolio of every 2024 Scheduler-track entry scores only 6.994, against 6.876 for No Man's Sky. The rest of the gap to best-known is fixed by the default planner. NMS's archived scheduler already uses Hungarian assignment plus a 'journey graph', it won again in 2026, and the track is centralized, so there is little headroom and a poor fit. (2) CFSTP/LFB (Zenodo 4764646). The archived results show CTS/D-CTS completing about 147-200 tasks at every task-to-agent ratio from 1 to 20 (98% at ratio 1, 6.7% at ratio 20 with 150 agents). The cause is that each agent starts at the station of one record whose deadline is that record's real attendance time. The benchmark is therefore near-degenerate, and any win would reduce to matching. (3) DTOP: 2-4 vehicles, centralized, 50% three-way ties, information-limited under high dynamism. (4) MG-TAPF: centralized optimal path finding, useful only as a reference. (5) CV_MRTA and the GACA protocol: static, fully known instances, so a planner replicated on every robot wins trivially. (6) PARTNR: 2 agents, allocation is not the bottleneck, and results depend on the LLM.
candidates.problem_formulation: The problem is single-task-robot, multi-robot-task (ST-MR) heterogeneous coalition scheduling. Agents belong to species with trait vectors. Task j has a requirement vector (additive AT, or binary BT), a location, a duration and, in Sadcher, precedence edges. Task j starts only when the summed traits of its coalition M_j cover the requirement, i.e. at the last member's arrival. The objective is to minimize makespan (all tasks done and all agents back at their depots), under the same global-communication assumption HeteroMRTA uses. The decentralized variant adds three things: per-robot local copies of the joint plan, lossy and delayed links (Gilbert-Elliott) with possible partitions, and stochastic travel and task durations revealed during execution.
candidates.algorithm: PLAN REPRESENTATION. Each task gets a real-valued global key k_j and a member set M_j. Each agent visits its tasks in increasing key order, and a single O(sum|M_j|) forward pass computes start times, waiting and makespan (precedence u->v is enforced as k_u<k_v plus start_v >= finish_u). Lemma: every such plan is deadlock-free. The smallest-key unfinished task always has all members free, because they have no pending smaller-key tasks. This replaces HeteroMRTA's Tmax=100 deadlock timeout. LOCAL SEARCH. Every robot runs anytime LNS with simulated-annealing or late-acceptance acceptance. The objective is lexicographic: (makespan, sum of completion times, total waiting). The sum-of-completion tie-breaker is there to escape makespan plateaus. Destroy operators: random; Shaw-related (location plus requirement similarity); worst-waiting (largest arrival skew within a coalition); critical path (tasks on the makespan-defining chain); agent-route segment; coalition-member swap between agents with equivalent traits. Repair: key-slot insertion with a greedy trait cover ordered by earliest arrival, plus regret-2 over slots. The prototype is /tmp/claude-0/-home-jovyan-dev-cbja/c781ca93-ceaa-4220-85a3-510892818ead/scratchpad/coalition_lns_pilot.py. DECENTRALIZATION (CBBA lineage, plan-level instead of per-task bids). Each robot searches with a different seed. Robots gossip their incumbent as {k_j, member bitmask}_j plus the objective and a version; this is under 4 KB for 250 tasks. A robot adopts a received plan when it is lexicographically better (max-consensus). The merge is monotone and idempotent, so it converges within network diameter times gossip period, even under loss, delay and reordering. Multiple robots therefore act as a parallel anytime solver. EXECUTION CONSISTENCY. Once any member departs toward task j, j's coalition and every smaller key on the involved routes are frozen as an execution prefix, analogous to CBBA reset. LNS may change only the unfrozen suffix. When partitions remerge, the union of frozen prefixes is a hard constraint. Duplicate starts are resolved by completion broadcast plus a lowest-ID keep rule. When realized delays arrive, a robot re-runs the forward pass and LNS-repairs the suffix. OPTIONAL SYSTEM-1: a small attention network, trained on the H100s to imitate LNS improvement moves in the style of NDS, scores which tasks to destroy. It is reported only as an ablation and is not needed for the claim.
candidates.why_it_should_win: The current best methods are one-pass constructive policies. HeteroMRTA RL decides the next task for each agent sequentially and can never revise an earlier commitment. RL(s.10) is only best-of-10 sampling. Sadcher imitates optimal solutions for 8 tasks and 3 robots and loses to Greedy at 20 robots once there are 70 or more tasks. Makespan in coalition tasks is dominated by synchronization idle time: the published average waiting time is 2.5-21 time units. LNS with waiting-aware and critical-path destroy operators attacks exactly that, and the exact forward-pass evaluator allows thousands of moves per second. Evidence: (a) on all 50 RALTestSet instances, centralized LNS at 4 s on one core gives mean makespan 23.44, against RL(s.10) 27.07 (-13.4%), RL(greedy) 29.02, SAS 29.74 and TACO 38.92. The LNS plans were replayed in HeteroMRTA's own environment with 0.0 evaluator discrepancy (scratchpad replay_check.py, rl_eval.json). (b) The published tables already show 11-18% headroom between RL(s.10) and CTAS-D wherever the MILP finishes: SA-BT kn=50 gives 22.87 vs 18.65, MA-AT kn=25/km=20 gives 23.67 vs 21.12, and SA-BT kn=9 gives 27.19 vs 23.66. On the medium and large sets where CTAS-D solves 0-40% of instances, LNS has no scaling wall. (c) Decentralized parallel seeds add search at fixed wall-clock, and max-consensus keeps that gain under loss. RL policies trained on global state have no loss model.
candidates.baselines_to_beat: With code: HeteroMRTA RL(g.) and RL(s.10) (Apache-2.0, checkpoint released). Published numbers: SA-BT kn=9 RL(s.10) 27.193, CTAS-D 23.658 (600 s), Greedy 32.733, SAS 27.408, TACO 35.068. SA-BT kn=50/km=50: RL(s.10) 22.871, CTAS-D 18.649 (96% success at 3600 s). SA-AT kn=15: RL(s.10) 57.454, CTAS-D 58.665 (34% success). MA-AT kn=25/km=50: RL(s.10) 46.983, CTAS-D 0% success. Our re-run on RALTestSet: RL(g.) 29.02, RL(s.10) 27.07, SAS 29.74, TACO 38.92. CTAS-D (Gurobi MILP; code in github.com/marmotlab/DCMRTA, MIT); a CP-SAT/HiGHS MILP will be built as an exact reference. Sadcher (github.com/jakbichler/Sadcher, no license, so run locally and unmodified): gap to MILP optimum S-Sadcher 3.8%, Sadcher 6.8%, S-HeteroMRTA 10.8%, Greedy 20.4%, HeteroMRTA 21.5%; Greedy beats S-Sadcher at N=20 once M>=70. Decentralized comparators, reimplemented: CBGA (Hunt et al. 2014), LNS-Auction (Sadeghi & Smith, Unmanned Systems 2017, which reports 16% average deviation from a centralized solver), central LNS plus broadcast with local fallback, and replicated same-seed LNS.
candidates.cbja_failure_mode_check: The margin does not come from a simple rule. The pilot's construction heuristic alone scores 29.70 (worse than RL), and the best of 10 constructions scores 26.68 (only -1.3% vs RL(s.10)). Full LNS scores 23.44 (-13.4%). The gain therefore comes from iterative improvement search, which no dispatch rule reproduces, and Greedy sits at 32.7. The gain is large and anchored: it matches the published RL-to-MILP gap of 11-18% and is backed by 50 or more paired instances per configuration. Honest caveat: on static, fully known instances the consensus layer contributes only parallel-seed search, about 1-3% (to be measured). We will not attribute the SOTA margin to consensus. The paper's claim is split: SOTA quality from key-ordered LNS, and robustness under loss and disturbances from the consensus and freeze protocol. In week 1 we will log how often consensus-LNS and replicated LNS end in different plans under loss. If the rate is under 5%, the decentralization section shrinks to an engineering note, as happened with CBJA.
candidates.cheap_pilot: Days 1-2, already partly done: 50 RALTestSet instances, LNS 23.44 vs RL(s.10) 27.07. Days 2-4: regenerate SA-BT kn=50/km=50 and MA-AT kn=25/km=50 (50 instances each, fixed seeds). Run RL(s.10) from the checkpoint on one H100 and LNS on one core with wall-clock equal to RL(s.10). Run a CP-SAT MILP (600 s) on the kn<=25 sets. Days 4-5: Sadcher 250K test split, LNS gap to optimum. Then the Sadcher scaling protocol at N=20, M in {100, 250} vs Greedy and S-Sadcher. Days 6-7: gossip max-consensus with 8 robots on RALTestSet under 50% Gilbert-Elliott loss, using the CBJA network kernel. KILL criteria, fixed in advance: any published configuration where matched-time LNS beats RL(s.10) by less than 5%; the Sadcher 250K gap not at least 2 points below S-Sadcher's 3.8%; or decentralized LNS more than 2% worse than central LNS at equal total CPU under 50% loss.
candidates.key_risks: (1) Novelty is moderate. 'Search beats one-shot learned policies on small combinatorial-optimization instances' is not surprising, and reviewers may call the learned baselines weak because they were compared only to ACO heuristics. Mitigation: a strong exact or CP-SAT reference, and wins at scales where the MILP fails. (2) Credibility of the benchmarks is medium: both come from single labs (RA-L 2025, MRS 2025) and neither has a leaderboard. (3) Unchecked newer competitors. A Semantic Scholar pass over HeteroMRTA's 43 citing papers turned up 'Makespan Minimization for Multi-Robot Task Allocation With Balance-Aware Pointerformer' (RA-L, Oct 2026, DOI 10.1109/LRA.2026.3728333) and DODRL-HMRTA (Neurocomputing 2026), whose content I could not read. They must be checked, and beaten if they use these sets. (4) Scoop risk: marmotlab or TU Delft could add search to their policies. (5) License friction: CTAS-D needs Gurobi, and Sadcher's code has no license (run it unmodified and cite it). (6) The decentralized benefit may be small on static instances (see the CBJA check above). (7) Another agent in this workflow is piloting the same arena (its scratchpad scripts are reused here), so candidates may overlap.
candidates.closest_prior_work: Verified from primary pages or PDFs: HeteroMRTA (Dai, Rai, Chiun, Cao, Sartoretti, RA-L 2025; decentralized RL assuming global communication; Tables I-III read from the PDF). SADCHER (Bichler et al., arXiv 2510.14851, MRS 2025; imitation learning from 250K MILP optima). LNS-Auction (Sadeghi & Smith, 'Heterogeneous Task Allocation and Sequencing via Decentralized Large Neighborhood Search', Unmanned Systems 2017; single-robot tasks, combinatorial auctions, no coalitions or synchronization; PDF read). Aswale & Pinciroli, IROS 2023 (arXiv 2306.11936; centralized coalition scheduling heuristic reaching 1x-2x of optimal). Gosrich et al., ICRA 2023 and T-RO 2025 (arXiv 2209.14417, 2509.15052; flow-based coalitions with precedence, own testbed). DGA (Patel et al., ICRA 2020; plan exchange). CBGA (Hunt et al. 2014). CF-HMRTA (JIRS 2025; bipartite matching; abstract via Crossref). Not found in any of these: a decentralized coalition LNS with deadlock-free key ordering and plan max-consensus evaluated on the HeteroMRTA or Sadcher sets. The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so novelty was checked through arXiv abstract pages, Semantic Scholar citation lists and Crossref only.
candidates.compute_and_timeline: Mostly CPU. The 13 HeteroMRTA configurations x 50 instances x 5 seeds x up to 30 s is about 27 CPU-hours. Sadcher's 500 instances plus the scaling sets are about 10 CPU-hours. Loss and noise sweeps are about 50 CPU-hours on 96 cores. One H100 runs the RL and Sadcher baselines, and optionally trains the System-1 destroy scorer (about 1 GPU-day). Timeline: 1 week pilot; 3 weeks for the full operator set, the precedence extension and the gossip/freeze protocol in a vectorized simulator; 2 weeks for the prespecified confirmation runs; 2 weeks of writing. About 8 weeks in total.
candidates.evaluation_protocol: Prespecify configurations, seeds, time budgets and kill margins before the confirmation runs (reuse the CBJA v10 workflow). The primary endpoint is paired per-instance makespan ratio against RL(s.10) at matched wall-clock (ours on 1 CPU core vs theirs on GPU), with a secondary endpoint at 10x budget. Report mean and median ratio, win rate, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, bootstrap 95% CIs and Holm correction across the 13 configurations, plus success rate and waiting time. Report exact MILP gaps where solvable and Sadcher optimum gaps. Development seeds and confirmation seeds are disjoint. Decentralized section: loss in {0, 10, 30, 50, 70}%, partition events and lognormal duration noise. Methods: central LNS plus broadcast, replicated LNS, consensus-LNS, and RL with stale state. Also report messages, bytes and plan-divergence rate.
candidates.reuse_from_cbja: The discrete-event network kernel (Gilbert-Elliott zones, ACK, TTL, relay; /home/jovyan/dev/cbja/cbja/network.py, kernel.py) for the lossy-link extension. The paired-bootstrap, Holm and TOST statistics and the prespecified confirmation-block workflow (scripts/analyze_v5.py, analyze_v10_confirm.py). The ProcessPool campaign runner. Lessons applied: identical infrastructure for every method, early decision-difference logging, and an exact reference bound. The Kev/DeBERTa judges are not used.

candidates.name: LiTCo: lifetime-triage coalition consensus for RoboCup Rescue
candidates.one_line: A CBBA/CBGA-lineage scheduler for disaster response under partial observability and lossy radio. Each coalition slot gets a bid gated on meeting the civilian's deadline, and anytime LNS repairs the bundles. The aim is to beat the RoboCup 2024 champion (AIT-Rescue, MIT code), whose allocation is nearest-first and deconflicts only against teammates in sight, on the official maps and communication profiles. The scheduler is validated at solver level on the original CFSTP benchmark against CFLA2 and CTS.
candidates.arena: PRIMARY: RoboCup Rescue Agent Simulation. Server: roborescue/rcrs-server (BSD-3). Maps and configs: the 12 official scenario directories in github.com/NONONOexe/rcrs-scenarios (berlin, eindhoven, istanbul, joao, kobe, montreal, ny, paris, sakae, sf, vc, test). Their comms.cfg files include degraded channels, for example input dropout p=0.1, output dropout 0.05, and channel failure p=0.1 or 1. Metrics: the official RCRS score (civilian survival and health, weighted by preserved building area), civilians alive, and buildings saved, compared with paired seeds per map. SECONDARY, a controlled solver-level SOTA: Ramchurn's original CFSTP random benchmark in github.com/lcpz/cfstp (MIT; EDF, CFLA, CFLA2, CTS; 100 instances x 300 tasks, 2-40 agents). Metric: percent of tasks completed. SANITY ONLY: the LFB-DCOP framework (Zenodo 4764646, MIT; CTS/D-CTS, DSA-SDP, FMS-ADVP). It is reported only as a check because its deadline structure is near-degenerate: about 150-200 completed tasks at every ratio. This arena was chosen over LoRR, DTOP and CV_MRTA because it is the only public, established arena where decentralization is necessary rather than cosmetic. It has private and partial observations, dynamically discovered tasks, radio with bandwidth caps and dropout, heterogeneous teams, coalition work, and hard deadlines (civilian death). A champion's code is public, which makes an externally anchored comparison possible.
candidates.problem_formulation: This is online, decentralized deadline-driven coalition formation (CFSTP with precedence) under partial observability. Rescue task c: workload is the buriedness, dug down additively by fire brigades each cycle. Its deadline d_c is the predicted death time minus the transport time to the nearest refuge. It has a precedence edge to a transport task done by an ambulance, and blocked roads create prerequisite clearance tasks for the police. Fire task f: a burning cluster whose workload grows over time and which is extinguished by fire-brigade coalitions with water-refill constraints. Tasks are discovered locally and shared over radio channels with byte budgets, dropout and failures. Objective: maximize the official score, with a lexicographic proxy of expected civilians saved and then building area preserved.
candidates.algorithm: LOCAL PLANNER. Each platoon agent keeps a task table built from perception and radio. Every cycle it runs a bounded-time anytime LNS over its believed task set to choose its bundle (an ordered task list) and the intended coalition slots. A rescue task counts only if the believed coalition finishes digging before d_c. Destroy operators: slack-critical tasks, spatial clusters, a single agent's bundle. Repair: insertion with coalition cover. CONSENSUS (CBGA lineage). Each task has K slots, and each slot holds (winner, bid, timestamp) with CBBA update and reset rules. The new part is the deadline-feasibility gate. A slot bid equals the marginal expected-saved value of adding this agent to the believed coalition, and it is zero unless the full coalition can meet the deadline. Coalitions that cannot finish in time therefore dissolve instead of wasting digging effort, which is the known failure of greedy and partial-coalition CBGA. LNS improvements are injected as fresh-timestamp bid batches. Agents commit to the head of the bundle when all its slots are won, or immediately when slack falls below travel time. MESSAGING. Only changed slot entries are sent, as packed (task, slot, bid, timestamp) tuples of about 8 bytes, ordered by slack to fit each channel's bandwidth. Stale entries are rebroadcast periodically to overcome dropout. The voice channel is used for co-located agents. Centre agents act only as relays. Inter-team coupling: police bids on clearance tasks carry the downstream rescue value. OPTIONAL SYSTEM-1: a small death-time regressor trained on simulator logs (HP, damage, buriedness trajectories) replaces AIT's heuristic LifetimeEstimator. It is an ablation, not core.
candidates.why_it_should_win: Reading the champion's code (NONONOexe/ait-rescue; README states RoboCup 2024 Agent Competition winner) pins down its weakness. Agents are statically partitioned into zones by one Hungarian matching (HungarianZoneAllocator.calc runs once). The ambulance and rescue target is the nearest candidate that passes a single-agent lifetime check (travel + transport <= lifetime). Deconfliction happens only against ambulances currently in sight (checkIsOptimalAssignee), and the agent then commits until the target becomes invalid (TargetingProcessor). There is no deliberate coalition digging to beat a deadline, no deadline-ordered sequencing across victims, no explicit claims when teammates are out of sight (so agents duplicate effort or leave gaps), and no cross-zone rebalancing. This is exactly the regime where CFSTP lookahead matters: agents scarce relative to tasks. On Ramchurn's benchmark archived in lcpz/cfstp, lookahead (CFLA2) beats the greedy and EDF rules by 11-18 points at 4-10 agents: 43.8% vs 32.3% (EDF) and 26.4% (CTS) at 4 agents, and 83.6% vs 65.3% and 63.9% at 10 agents. It converges with EDF and CTS only when agents are plentiful (20+ agents, about 92-96%). Explicit timestamped claims make the allocation robust to the dropout profiles, which AIT's in-sight rule ignores.
candidates.baselines_to_beat: AIT-Rescue 2024 champion (MIT, github.com/NONONOexe/ait-rescue), run unmodified. It has no published per-map scores, so we generate paired numbers. RoboCup 2025 results for context (rescuesim.robocup.org): Timrad 63, AIT-Rescue 58, 3Rakshak 48 rank points. Timrad's code was not found. Also: AIT plus simple rules (min-slack/EDF target choice; per-cycle Hungarian at the centre agent with broadcast), ADF sample agents, the RRS DCOP module (uiiaoo/dcop.rrs-adf), reimplemented CBGA, and a central CFSTP solver at the centre agents with local fallback. CFSTP benchmark (lcpz/cfstp, MIT; results/ramchurns-benchmark.txt; 300 tasks), % tasks completed: 2 agents CFLA 27.24, CFLA2 23.68, EDF 16.17, CTS 9.41. 8 agents CFLA2 74.30, EDF 57.24, CTS 52.25. 10 agents CFLA2 83.59, EDF 65.33, CTS 63.88. 16 agents CFLA2 89.10, CTS 86.94. 40 agents CTS 98.15. The CCF paper (arXiv 2003.13806) claims up to 10% more tasks than CFLA2. LFB-DCOP: D-CTS completes 3.79% more than DSA-SDP (EUMAS 2021).
candidates.cbja_failure_mode_check: The main danger is that the gain reduces to a slack or EDF rule, which is the CBJA trap: a clever selector that equals a deadline rule. We guard against it in three ways. (1) 'AIT + min-slack/EDF' and 'AIT + centre Hungarian' are first-class baselines, and SOTA is claimed only if LiTCo beats the best simple rule by a prespecified margin, with a TOST-style equivalence test run the other way. (2) We log from week 1 how often LiTCo's committed target, coalition size and sequence differ from the EDF rule. The mechanism EDF cannot express is coalition sizing (two or three fire brigades digging one victim to beat d_c) and multi-victim sequencing. If fewer than 10% of decisions differ, we kill it. (3) On the CFSTP benchmark the gap between lookahead and rules is 11-18 points exactly where agents are scarce, so the claimed mechanism has independent evidence of size. The gain comes from joint coalition and sequence optimization, not from a gate threshold. The gate only removes infeasible coalitions and carries no free parameter.
candidates.cheap_pilot: Week 1. (a) Build rcrs-server and ait-rescue headless; Java 11+ is present. Run AIT on 4 official maps (sakae, kobe, paris, ny) x 5 seeds with their shipped comm configs. (b) Instrument civilian deaths into four classes: never discovered, discovered but unreachable (blocked), discovered and reachable but died waiting (allocation-attributable), and died in fire. For the third class, solve an offline clairvoyant CFSTP (CP-SAT) over each victim's discovery time, buriedness and lifetime with the actually available fire brigades and ambulances, to bound the civilians savable by allocation alone. (c) Plug an EDF/min-slack rule into AIT's HumanDetector and measure the score change. (d) Run a quick LNS-CFSTP solver on lcpz/cfstp's generator at 4, 8, 10 and 16 agents vs CFLA2 and CTS. KILL criteria: oracle-savable allocation-attributable deaths below 5% of civilians on average; EDF capturing at least 70% of the oracle headroom; or the LNS-CFSTP solver less than 5 points above max(CFLA2, CTS) at 4-10 agents.
candidates.key_risks: (1) Credibility. The RCRS community is small (3 finalist teams in 2025, results given as rank points), ML and robotics venues discount it, the 2025 champion's code was not found, and no per-map scores are published. The SOTA claim is therefore 'beats the best published champion code on official maps', which is weaker than a leaderboard. (2) Margin uncertainty. The score also depends on search, perception, pathing and fire modules, so allocation gains could be diluted to a few points. The pilot measures this before any build. (3) Engineering. Java ADF modules must respect radio byte budgets. Each simulation takes about 5-15 min, which is feasible with 96 cores. (4) Noise in fire spread and dropout requires about 20-30 paired seeds per map. (5) The CBJA lesson that central planning wins with good links: a centre-based CFSTP could beat decentralized consensus on low-loss maps. We report both and claim only what holds. (6) Novelty is moderate. CFSTP was motivated by RCRS ambulances (Ramchurn et al., AAMAS 2010), max-sum DCOP was applied in RCRS (Ramchurn et al., Computer Journal 2010), and binary max-sum for inter-team allocation (Pujol-Gonzalez et al., AAMAS 2015) is recalled from memory and was not verified this session. The contribution must be the deadline-gated slot consensus under lossy radio plus a measured win over modern champion code.
candidates.closest_prior_work: CFSTP and CFLA (Ramchurn, Polukarov, Farinelli, Truong, Jennings, AAMAS 2010). CCF/CTS (Capezzuto, Tarapore, Ramchurn, arXiv 2003.13806). D-CTS on LFB data (EUMAS 2021, arXiv 2106.00379; PDF read; 5 citing papers, none on the benchmark). DCOP max-sum in RoboCup Rescue (Ramchurn et al., The Computer Journal 2010, doi 10.1093/comjnl/bxq022). CBGA (Hunt et al., Cognitive Computation 2014). CBBA (Choi, Brunet, How, T-RO 2009). AIT-Rescue 2024 champion code, including the 'distributed coordination strategy' from a PhD thesis per its README (source read). Semantic Scholar citation lists of the CFSTP papers show no follow-up benchmarking on LFB or RCRS since 2021. A full novelty search was impossible because the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted, so arXiv abstract pages, the Semantic Scholar API, Crossref and GitHub were used.
candidates.compute_and_timeline: CPU only. RCRS: 12 maps x 25 seeds x 5 methods x 2 comm profiles is about 3,000 simulations x about 10 min, roughly 21 h at 24 concurrent runs on 96 cores. The CFSTP benchmark takes minutes. The optional lifetime regressor takes under 1 GPU-hour. Timeline: 1 week pilot and kill decision; 4 weeks to implement the Java modules (consensus tables, message packing, LNS-CFSTP) and port the solver; 2 weeks for the prespecified confirmation campaign; 2 weeks of writing. About 9 weeks in total.
candidates.evaluation_protocol: Prespecify maps, comm profiles (shipped official ones plus a stress profile), seeds and margins. Development maps and seeds are separate from confirmation seeds. Primary endpoint: paired official score difference against AIT-2024, per map and pooled, with a bootstrap CI and Holm correction across maps. Secondary endpoints: civilians alive, building area, messages and bytes, and a decision-difference rate against the EDF rule. Ablations: without the deadline gate, without LNS repair, without claims (AIT deconfliction), a centralized centre-agent solver, and with the learned lifetime model. CFSTP benchmark: 100 instances per agent count from 2 to 40, paired vs EDF, CFLA, CFLA2 and CTS on identical generated instances, plus a CP-SAT exact gap on small instances.
candidates.reuse_from_cbja: The stats and prespecification workflow (paired bootstrap, Holm, TOST; analyze_v10_confirm.py). The CBJA finding that the incremental deadline rule matched VOC, reused here as a mandatory simple-rule baseline. The Gilbert-Elliott link model, for an optional extra stress profile beyond RCRS's native dropout and failure. The ProcessPool campaign runner, adapted to launch RCRS runs. Kev and the NLI judges are not needed. The small System-1 slot goes to an optional learned death-time regressor instead.
candidates.target_venue: AAMAS 2028 main track or IJCAI 2027. Alternatives: JAAMAS, or the RoboCup Symposium as a companion paper.

candidates.name: SyncCoal-CBBA: max-plus coalition consensus with deadlock-free ordering and decentralized coalition LNS
candidates.one_line: A CBBA-lineage decentralized allocator for tasks that need a multi-robot coalition to be present at the same time. It has three layers: robots agree on start times through a max-plus timing layer that tolerates loss (a CRDT); a consensus global task order makes deadlock impossible; and coalition-level ruin-and-recreate moves improve the plan and commit only when every affected robot confirms. Target: 12-16% lower makespan than the strongest published method with code (HeteroMRTA RL) and than Sadcher, while keeping those gains under lossy links.
candidates.arena: Primary: the HeteroMRTA benchmark (Dai et al., IEEE RA-L 10(3) 2025, github.com/marmotlab/HeteroMRTA, Apache-2.0). It ships 50 instances in RALTestSet (15 robots, 20 tasks, 5 traits) plus a generator for the paper's other 11 sets (SA-BT, SA-AT, MA-AT, 9-50 robots, 20-50 tasks). Metrics: mean makespan (primary), success rate, average waiting time and compute time, all measured in the benchmark's own simulator. candidates.algorithm: Model (HeteroMRTA/Sadcher semantics): robot i has a trait vector c_i. Task j has a requirement r_j, a duration d_j, a location, and optional precedence edges. j starts at s_j = max over coalition members of their arrival once the summed traits cover r_j. Robots return to their depots, and the objective is makespan. (1) ORDER LAYER: every task carries a consensus key k_j (a real number with an ID tiebreak), and every robot's route must be sorted by key. The plan graph (route edges + synchronization + precedence) is therefore acyclic by construction. Keys change only inside committed moves. (2) TIMING LAYER: each robot computes its arrival at task j locally from its predecessor's finish time and gossips (epoch_j, a_ij). The start time s_j is a join over (epoch, max) pairs. This max-plus fixpoint is idempotent, commutative and monotone, so it converges within depth(DAG) delivered rounds under loss, duplication and reordering. Every robot therefore knows exact start times and the current makespan (gossiped route completion times) without a snapshot. (3) CONSTRUCTION: a CBBA-style auction over requirement 'slots' (a bid is the negative earliest arrival). Consensus per slot uses winner/bid/timestamp tables. A coalition is committed only when coverage is complete, through a two-phase prepare/ack/commit among its members with a lease; the key is set at the commit timestamp. Robots never travel to a task whose coalition is uncommitted. (4) IMPROVEMENT (anytime): each robot periodically proposes a coalition ruin-and-recreate move on its versioned replica of the committed plan. It removes q related tasks (Shaw relatedness: space, time, shared members) from all their coalitions. It reinserts each removed task by best synchronized insertion: over candidate key slots it computes each robot's arrival from the timing layer, picks a greedy trait cover (with noise), and evaluates the exact makespan on the plan DAG. The move is accepted if (makespan, sorted completion-time vector) strictly improves in leximax order. Proposals are arbitrated MGM-k style: each robot locks the best-gain proposal that touches it. A move commits through 2PC with optimistic version validation of the write set plus the timing cone (the robots sharing coalitions with the moved tasks). Tasks inside a commit horizon (next task, or ETA below tau) are frozen. (5) EXECUTION UNDER DELAYS AND LOSS: if a partner misses its lease at a task, the task is reinserted as a committed move, so waiting is bounded. Guarantees: (Q1) deadlock-freedom, from acyclicity through the global order; (Q2) the timing layer converges under any fair-lossy channel (CRDT); (Q3) coalition atomicity, so no robot waits for a partner that never committed; (Q4) monotone leximax improvement for serialized commits, and convergence with probability 1 to a local optimum over k-coalition exchanges. Complexity is about O(q * slots * |plan|) per proposal. Optional System-1 or H100 add-on (not required): an NDS-style learned destroy selector trained on generated instances.
candidates.why_it_should_win: Mechanism: HeteroMRTA-RL, Sadcher and Greedy decide online and sequentially. Each robot picks its next task at decision time and never revises a coalition afterwards. Makespan under synchronization depends on joint coalition and order decisions (who waits for whom), and one-shot constructive policies cannot correct these. Local search over coalitions with exact max-plus makespan evaluation does correct them. Measured this session on the 50 shipped RALTestSet instances, all replayed inside HeteroMRTA's own simulator (plan replay matches my evaluator exactly, 100% success): TACO 38.92, Greedy 32.42, SAS 29.74, RL(g.) 29.02, RL(s.10) 27.07 (released checkpoint, 3.87 s per instance). An unoptimized single-thread Python centralized coalition-LNS scored 23.53 at 4 s (paired ratio to RL(s.10) 0.868, 95% bootstrap CI [0.856, 0.879], better on 50/50 instances) and 22.62 at 30 s (0.836 [0.825, 0.847]). The decentralized version should keep most of this gain for three reasons. Moves are local: coalitions have 2-4 members, so a commit needs only those robots. The timing CRDT gives each proposer exact start times without global synchronization. And robots run moves in parallel (about N-fold search throughput). Under lossy links the baselines have no protection: HeteroMRTA assumes global communication, and agents with stale state commit to coalitions that never form (the env's 200 s wait-timeout deadlocks). SyncCoal's ordering and 2PC rule this out by construction.

candidates.name: CERT-LNS: consensus-certified anytime large-neighborhood search over CBBA ownership tables for makespan and time-window missions under lossy links
candidates.one_line: A decentralized anytime improvement layer on top of GCBBA/ACBBA. Robots propose multi-robot string-removal ruin-and-recreate moves from their neighbourhood's versioned routes; moves are arbitrated MGM-k style and committed atomically by version-checked two-phase commit with leases. The result is provably conflict-free under any message loss and monotone in the leximax makespan, and it converges with probability 1 to a local optimum over k-robot exchanges. Target: 15-25% lower realized makespan than the best published decentralized allocator where tasks-per-robot is at least 8.
candidates.arena: Primary: the CV_MRTA_Benchmark simulator and protocol (Lott & Honary, arXiv 2609.13711; github.com/jlott22/CV_MRTA_Benchmark, all 6 baselines' code). Configuration: MinMax (makespan) at its released scale grid (6/8/12/16 robots x 25/50/75/100 targets, 19x19 grid; published per-trial data under ideal links), extended to its 24 impaired conditions (Bernoulli, Gilbert-Elliott, Rayleigh) and to a dynamic variant where 30-50% of targets are revealed online to the nearest robot only (contributed upstream). The code has no license, so written permission from the authors is required. Metric: realized max robot steps (MinMax) as the paired ratio to the best published allocator per cell, plus publications per team step and per-robot compute. Secondary, MILP-anchored: the GACA protocol (arXiv 2608.15884; 5-20 agents, 10-80 tasks, MILP reference), percent of optimum (MinMax and MinSum) against Bernoulli loss rate. Tertiary: TOPTW (Righini-Salani / Montemanni-Gambardella, BKS at KU Leuven) as a static time-window anchor.
candidates.algorithm: State: every task j has (owner, version v_j). Each robot gossips a compact route summary (ordered task IDs, versions, completion-time estimate, heartbeat), using CBBA-style timestamps and relaying. SEED: GCBBA with the Repeated-Path-Times utility (Kha et al., ECAI 2025) when links allow, otherwise ACBBA. Tasks never assigned stay in an open pool, auctioned CBBA-style. PROPOSE (every delta seconds, each robot i): pick a destroy set S by SISR string removal (spatially adjacent strings) from the routes of i and its current neighbours N_i. Repair with greedy-with-blinks insertion restricted to an affected robot set A (subset of {i} plus N_i, |A| at most k, k in {2,3}), respecting time windows. Compute the exact delta on A: the MinSum change, or the leximax change of A's route completion vector for MinMax (sufficient for a global leximax improvement, because routes are independent in ST-SR-TA). Broadcast P = (delta, A, read-versions, new routes). ARBITRATE (MGM-k): each robot in A locks the proposal with the best delta that involves it within the round (ties broken by ID). COMMIT: 2PC (prepare/ack/commit) among A with version validation and a lease timeout; abort on any missing ack; commit bumps versions. EXECUTION: robots always execute the committed route. Tasks in the commit horizon (next task, or ETA below tau) are frozen. DYNAMIC: a newly discovered task is inserted immediately (cheapest insertion) into the discoverer's route, so it is owned with no global consensus; LNS later moves it. FAILURE: an owner whose lease expires returns its tasks to the pool. Guarantees: (P1) safety: under arbitrary loss, duplication and reordering, every task has at most one owner and none are silently dropped. (P2) monotone MinSum / leximax MinMax; commits on disjoint robot sets compose. (P3) under fair-lossy links (per-message delivery probability at least q > 0), with probability 1 it reaches a local optimum over k-exchanges in finite time, and the commit rate is at least q^(2k) per proposal. Loss therefore automatically shrinks the effective neighbourhood arity; the loss-adaptive depth reported in arXiv 2609.06273 emerges without a hand-set rule. (P4) never worse than its seed, so it inherits GCBBA's 50% bound when that holds. (P5) anytime: no global convergence is needed before acting.
candidates.why_it_should_win: Mechanism: every published decentralized allocator in the arena either builds the plan greedily (CBAA/ACBBA/HIPC/DMCHBA) or searches team plans globally, at heavy cost and fragile under loss (DGA: 1.3-23 s per call, 5/100 viable pre-allocations at p=0.5). None ever revises the robot-to-task assignment once consensus holds. For makespan with many tasks per robot, balancing the assignment is exactly what greedy gets wrong. Measured this session on CV_MRTA-distribution instances (same generator and start layout, different seeds, collision-free Manhattan relaxation, 8 instances per cell): min-max-aware greedy insertion followed by near-optimal per-robot re-sequencing (the trivial fix) is still 1.13x (25 targets), 1.21x (50) and 1.25x (100) the near-optimal makespan at 6 robots, but only 1.03-1.10x at 16 robots. The benchmark's released scale data (ideal links) shows the best realized MinMax at 6 robots is 1.17x / 1.29x / 1.36x this reference at 25/50/100 targets, and 1.04-1.16x at 16 robots. Inter-robot LNS moves are what close the assignment part of this gap. Certified commits keep the gain under loss, because a lost message only aborts one move: the plan never becomes inconsistent, unlike ACBBA/PI reallocation, which thrashes.

candidates.name: DiSCo: Distilled-Solver Coalition Consensus (heterogeneous coalition missions)
candidates.one_line: A small per-robot attention policy, imitation-trained with DAgger from a centralized ALNS/CP-SAT teacher and run inside CBGA-style coalition-table consensus over lossy links. Target: at least 10% lower makespan than HeteroMRTA RL at matched real-time budgets, and at least 20% under 30-50% packet loss.
candidates.arena: Primary: the HeteroMRTA RA-L 2025 protocol (marmotlab/HeteroMRTA, Apache-2.0), covering the SA-BT, SA-AT and MA-AT settings (9-50 agents, 20-50 tasks, 3-5 species, 5 skills). The metric is makespan, plus success rate and waiting time, at matched per-instance wall time. The repo ships RALTestSet, which is only ONE setting: 50 instances with 15 robots and 20 tasks, plus CTAS-D, SAS and TACO solutions. The other settings are regenerated with the repo's generator using frozen seeds, and every baseline is re-run on them. Secondary: SADCHER's scaling protocol (MRS 2025; N=3/5/20 robots, M up to 250 tasks, with precedence; dataset CC BY 4.0). Robustness axis: the same instances under Bernoulli, Gilbert-Elliott and range-limited links with latency, where every method uses the identical channel and table-merge infrastructure.
candidates.problem_formulation: There are n agents of k_s species, each with a binary trait vector c_a in {0,1}^5, and m tasks. Each task has a position, a duration d_j and a requirement r_j in {0,1,2}^5. For additive tasks (AT) the coalition's traits must sum to at least r_j; for binary tasks (BT) each required skill must be covered. A task starts only when its covering coalition is physically present, and every agent returns to its species depot. The objective is to minimize makespan, the maximum working time of any agent. Execution is decentralized and event-driven: each agent picks its next task when it finishes the current one. It knows its own state exactly. It sees task status and teammates' claims and states only through messages on a lossy, range-limited channel. Ideal channel = the published protocol. Degraded channel = our pre-registered extension.
candidates.algorithm:
(1) Teacher. A centralized anytime solver on the full state. ALNS over agent routes with event-based start-time propagation. Destroy operators: random, spatially related, coalition-breaking, worst-waiting. Repair: synchronized greedy and regret-2 insertion, with simulated-annealing acceptance. CP-SAT polishes instances with 20 tasks or fewer. It runs 30-300 s per instance on 96 cores, is checked against CTAS-D where CTAS-D solves, and labels about 150k instances from 9 to 100 agents.
(2) Student pi_theta, one per agent, under 20 ms on one CPU core. A HeteroMRTA-style attention encoder over the task graph and the agent graph, built from the agent's local belief. Task features: remaining requirement after committed claims, predicted start time, status age. Agent features: teammates' last-known state and message age. Heads: (a) the agent's next task; (b) each teammate's next-task distribution, used as implicit claims when messages are lost; (c) a critic V_phi for remaining makespan.
(3) Consensus layer, CBGA/CBBA lineage. Each agent keeps a per-task coalition table of claims (agent, ETA, timestamp). Tables merge monotonically, keeping the maximum stamp per claimant. When a task is oversubscribed, claims are sorted by ETA and the minimal covering prefix is kept; agents outside it are released and re-decide. Start time S_j is the maximum ETA over the cover. A commitment lock applies within delta travel time of arrival, and a deadlock guard releases a claim when the cover is unfillable for longer than tau.
(4) Runtime decision. Sample K=10 candidates from pi_theta. Score each with a short belief-space rollout of pi_theta, or with V_phi. Claim the best and broadcast it.
(5) Training. Behavior cloning on teacher next-task labels. Then 5-10 DAgger rounds: student rollouts in the lossy channel simulator (p_loss ~ U[0,0.7], Gilbert-Elliott bursts, range and latency), with the teacher re-solving the TRUE state with committed prefixes fixed (5-10 s warm starts). Optional POMO-style RL fine-tuning with HeteroMRTA's flashforward. Scale curriculum from 9 to 100 agents.
candidates.why_it_should_win:
1. Supervision quality. SADCHER shows that imitating near-optimal schedules beats REINFORCE on the same instance class: 6.8% gap to the MILP optimum, versus 21.5% for HeteroMRTA. SADCHER lost at scale only because it had no demonstrations there (its own stated limitation). An ALNS teacher supplies demonstrations at every HeteroMRTA size.
2. Measured headroom. On the published tables HeteroMRTA RL(s.10) is 15-23% worse than CTAS-D wherever CTAS-D solves. SA-BT kn=9/km=20: 27.19 vs 23.66. kn=25/km=20: 20.07 vs 16.49. kn=50/km=50: 22.87 vs 18.65. A student within 5-8% of a teacher that roughly matches CTAS-D would therefore land 8-15% below RL.
3. Communication. HeteroMRTA's formulation assumes observations of all agents update instantly (global communication). Under loss its agents oversubscribe tasks and strand coalitions, and the wait time and Tmax=100 timeouts grow. Monotone table merges, commitment locks and predicted teammate claims (trained under dropout via DAgger) keep coalitions consistent.
4. Test-time search (K samples plus the critic) matches RL(s.10)'s search budget, but starts from a better prior.

candidates.name: LSPA: Learned Shadow-Price Asynchronous Auction for lifelong multi-robot scheduling
candidates.one_line: Each agent bids in an asynchronous epsilon-auction with reduced-cost bids built from two learned models: a GNN that predicts regional shadow prices (the anticipatory value of a free agent in each region) and a congestion-aware travel-time model. Monotone prices keep the auction correct under stale or dropped messages. Target: beat the LoRR 2024/2026 scheduling winner on the official instances.
candidates.arena: League of Robot Runners Task-Scheduling track, via Start-Kit v3.1.0 (MIT) with the default planner and executor fixed. It uses the 10 official 2024 main-round instances (up to 10k agents; best-known solutions and the archived winner code are public), plus GRAND's map suite (warehouse, room and maze at 100-500 agents, 50 seeds each) for statistics, plus the 2026 execution-delay instances once they are archived. Metrics: tasks finished and the normalized track score, within the official per-step time limits. Robustness axis (our extension): agent-to-agent communication radius and Bernoulli/Gilbert-Elliott loss, where each agent's scheduler input is its own belief.
candidates.problem_formulation:
Lifelong multi-agent pickup-and-delivery (MAPD) scheduling. At each tick new errand tasks join the pool. The scheduler proposes agent-to-task assignments, and reassignment is allowed until the first errand starts. The fixed PIBT-based planner moves the agents. The goal is to maximize tasks finished over the horizon under a 1 s per-step compute limit shared with the planner.
Decentralized formulation: agent i holds belief B_i. It knows its own state exactly, sees the task board (broadcast by a WMS, or range-limited in the lossy variant), holds gossip-estimated regional aggregates with ages, and hears neighbours' claims over lossy links. Ideal links = the official benchmark.
candidates.algorithm:
(1) Region graph G_R: about 64 tiles per region, corridor-aware.
(2) Price GNN f_theta on G_R. Per-region inputs: free and arriving agents, open pickup and delivery counts, planner-wait congestion counts, time, and a geometry embedding. Output: lambda_r, the value of one extra free agent at r over horizon H. Each agent evaluates it on its local K-hop belief in under 1 ms on CPU.
(3) Travel-time model g_psi(r_from, r_to, congestion), regressed on start-kit logs with the default planner.
(4) Bids: u_ij = beta - g(i->pickup_j) - g(pickup_j->delivery_j) + lambda_r(delivery_j) - lambda_r(i). This is a one-step ADP / reduced-cost bid. Idle agents may also bid on virtual rebalancing moves to region r, with value lambda_r - lambda_r(i) - g(i->r).
(5) Asynchronous Bertsekas epsilon-auction among agents within radius r_c. Task prices are monotone within a version. Agent i bids for argmax_j (u_ij - p_j) over its k nearest candidates and raises p_j by (best - second best + epsilon). Highest bid wins, with ties broken by timestamp and id. Prices warm-start from the previous tick. Reassignment uses hysteresis, and stale bids stay safe because prices only rise.
(6) Training, in three stages. (a) Supervised: regress lambda onto hindsight duals of a time-expanded regional min-cost flow with known future arrivals. (b) End-to-end PPO or SAC on theta with reward = tasks finished, in a JAX-vectorized grid simulator with a PIBT-like surrogate planner on the H100s, randomizing maps, densities and loss. (c) Validation and light fine-tuning in the real start-kit on the CPU farm.
(7) Engineering: a C++ implementation targeting 200 ms or less per step at 10k agents.
candidates.why_it_should_win:
1. Anticipation measurably matters here. In GRAND's own ablation (200 agents, no reassignment), learned guidance scores 17,916 vs 16,433 for uniform guidance (+9%). Naive demand-based guidance does worse (14,910), so the value is not a trivial demand rule. GRAND beats the LoRR 2024 winner by +10.7% with reassignment (20,752 vs 18,752) and +38% without. NeurADP (arXiv 1911.08842) gets +16% over myopic matching from learned values.
2. Congestion-aware costs help. Flow-based TA gains 10-16% over greedy from congestion-aware edges, while GRAND's matching uses plain distances.
3. Solution structure. An epsilon-auction on reduced costs solves the whole assignment problem epsilon-optimally with prices. GRAND instead splits it into an inter-region flow plus per-region Hungarian matching, and its per-step time grows from about 50 ms at 100 agents to about 250 ms at 500 agents. Warm-started auctions change few assignments per tick, which is what makes the official 10k-agent instances fit the budget.
4. Asynchronous auctions converge with outdated prices (Bertsekas and Castanon 1991), so the method degrades gracefully under loss, where centralized schedulers need the full state.

candidates.name: FRESH-Rescue: freshness-priced team messaging and target holding for RoboCup Rescue under the official degraded-comm profiles
candidates.one_line: A decentralized coordination layer for heterogeneous rescue teams of 30-150 agents. It prices every fact by (value to the teammates who lack it) x (probability it is still true, given its age) per byte of shared radio. Agents coordinate who reports what, relay the facts that neighbours lack, and choose between holding a target, verifying it, switching or deferring. The layer is dropped into the RoboCup 2024 champion's own code, replacing only its communication and targeting modules, and is scored on the official RCRS scenarios under the official communication profiles.
candidates.arena: RoboCup Rescue Simulation, Agent Simulation League (an external, long-running benchmark with official scoring). Server: github.com/roborescue/rcrs-server (BSD-3, pushed 2026-07-26). Official scenarios: github.com/NONONOexe/rcrs-scenarios, 11 real maps (berlin, eindhoven, istanbul, joao, kobe, montreal, ny, paris, sakae, sf, vc) with 30-150 platoon agents, 100-413 civilians and 190-369 steps. I verified the official communication profiles by cloning the scenarios repo (scratchpad rcrs/). All profiles give the whole team ONE radio channel of 4,000 bytes per step plus 30 m voice (1 message of at most 256 B per step, 10% dropout). Profiles: comms-01-full, 02-high (radio input failure 0.1, output dropout 0.05), 03-midle (0.2/0.1), 04-low (0.3/0.15), 05-fullJammer (radio failure 1.0), 06-noneChannel (voice only). Primary metric: the official RSL21 score (civilian health plus building damage) per map. Secondary metrics: civilians alive, buildings saved, radio bytes discarded by the kernel, information latency (time from first sighting to first responder knowing), and wasted or duplicate trips.
candidates.algorithm: Keep all of AIT-Rescue 2024 (perception, path planning, clearing, clustering, extinguish and rescue tactics). Replace its MessageCoordinator, VoiceMessageManager and target detectors with five parts. (1) Versioned fact store. A fact is (entity, quantized attributes, t_obs, observer, version) with a compact delta encoding. Per-region Bloom-filter digests ride on every message so that receivers can estimate who lacks what. (2) System-1 validity hazards: tiny CPU models (LightGBM or 2-layer MLP, under 1 ms), trained on the kernel's ground-truth logs from about 3k simulated runs, leave-one-map-out. h_civ = P(civilian alive and unrescued at arrival | HP, damage, buriedness, age, nearby fire, known claimants). h_bld = P(building still salvageable | fieriness, temperature, age, neighbours). h_road = P(blockade still present | repair cost, age, police nearby). h_claim = P(claimant still pursuing | claim age, claimant state, distance). (3) Team-level channel arbitration, a CBBA-lineage consensus reached by construction. Every agent hears the same radio traffic, so a per-channel shadow price lambda_c, updated by dual ascent on last step's load and discards, is common knowledge. For each candidate fact f an agent computes V(f) = sum over recipients j of P(j lacks f | digests) x dU_j(f), where dU is the hazard-weighted change in the recipient's decision. It sends f only if V(f)/bytes(f) > lambda_c AND it is f's designated reporter (closest known observer, hash tie-break). Otherwise it holds; if f is not heard by t+1, the next-ranked observer sends it (ask again). This removes both oversubscription and redundant reporting. Voice uses the same rule over 30 m neighbours, plus anti-entropy relaying of facts neighbours lack and store-carry-forward toward centres and refuges when the radio is jammed. (4) Targeting as hold, verify, switch or defer. Each platoon maximizes h(fact, age+ETA) x U(target) - travel - duplication risk (sum over claimants of h_claim). VERIFY (travel to observe a stale, high-stakes region) has an explicit travel cost and value = expected decision improvement. Switching carries sunk-progress hysteresis. Compact claims (task, claimant, bid, t) are resolved CBBA-style (highest bid, id tie-break) with age discounting through h_claim. (5) Optional authentication: a truncated HMAC per bundle. It is a cost only; no claim rests on it.
candidates.why_it_should_win: There are three concrete levers, each verified in code. (i) Channel oversubscription. rcrs-server RadioChannel.pushImpl adds up bytes from all senders and discards every message beyond the channel's per-step bandwidth, first come first served. In every official profile the team has one 4,000 B radio channel, roughly 27-40 B per agent per step on 100-150-agent maps. Yet AIT's ChannelGroup lets each agent budget the full 4,000 B for itself and orders messages only by a static per-class priority. So the team oversubscribes, the kernel drops arbitrary (often critical) messages, and several observers re-report the same burning building. Team-level shadow-price arbitration with designated reporters raises the useful information per byte. This mirrors CBJA's one real algorithmic gain, charging per new text, which was worth +20 to +31 raw points. (ii) Information islands. Under fullJammer and noneChannel, voice is the only medium. AIT's voice relay follows a fixed 7-level priority list and ignores what neighbours already know. Digest-driven anti-entropy plus store-carry-forward cut information latency. This is the lever CBJA identified (42 of 48 severe-link violations followed notices that were never received) but never built. (iii) Staleness. Civilians' HP decays and fires spread, so stale reports send ambulances and brigades to dead, already-rescued or burnt-out targets. Hazard discounting and claim ageing remove those wasted trips. A realistic target is +10-20% relative official score over AIT-2024 on the degraded profiles and non-inferiority on full or high. The pilot bounds this with an oracle-information run before any real build.
candidates.baselines_to_beat: (1) AIT-Rescue 2024: champion of the RoboCup 2024 Agent Competition, 2nd in 2025 (final Timrad 63, AIT-Rescue 58, 3Rakshak 48; rescuesim.robocup.org 2025 results page, totals only, no per-map scores). Code: github.com/NONONOexe/ait-rescue, MIT, last push 2025-09-26, maintained for PhD-thesis reproducibility; 85 Java files, cloned and inspected. Paper: Ando, Maeda, Uehara, 'Designing a Rescue Strategy Emphasizing Distributed Control in RoboCupRescue Simulation', LNCS 2025, doi 10.1007/978-3-031-85859-8_37. (2) ADF sample team: roborescue/adf-sample-agent-java, BSD-3. (3) The DCOP / max-sum module in the official open-source list: github.com/uiiaoo/dcop.rrs-adf. (4) Timrad (2025 champion) and 3Rakshak: no public code, so request their competition binaries from the teams or organizers (availability unverified). (5) Pre-registered simple-rule variants of AIT: newest-first plus deduplication, and a fair bandwidth share (4000/N bytes each). No per-map published numbers exist, so every comparison is a paired re-run of the published code on identical seeds.
candidates.cbja_failure_mode_check: CBJA's value-of-computation selector collapsed to a deadline test because a query cost nothing and rival persistence was always below 1. Here, bytes have a positive shadow price that binds (one shared 4,000 B channel for 30-150 agents), and VERIFY carries an explicit travel cost, so the Proposition-1 argument does not go through by construction. It still has to be checked empirically: (a) log the Kendall tau and the byte overlap between FRESH's per-step send set and the 'newest-first + dedup' rule, and stop if they agree on more than 90% of bytes; (b) log how often FRESH's target choice differs from AIT's. Headroom is measured before building anything (oracle-information bound in the pilot). There is no uneven infrastructure: both arms share every AIT module except communication and targeting, and an 'encoding-only' ablation isolates pure packing gains so they are not credited to the algorithm. The team sizes (30-150 agents) and 11 external maps with fixed official profiles avoid CBJA's tiny, self-designed missions.
candidates.cheap_pilot: Days 1-2: build NONONOexe/rcrs-docker (server plus AIT-Rescue; MIT, cloned) and run AIT on 4 maps (kobe, sakae, ny, paris) x 3 profiles (full, midle, noneChannel) x 5 seeds = 60 runs. The kernel waits the full think time every step (TimedCommandCollector), so a run takes about 4-7 min plus startup; use 8 concurrent runs with pinned cores. Days 3-4: parse the kernel logs for radio bytes discarded ('Discarding message on channel'), the duplicate-report rate, information latency for buried civilians, and trips that end at dead or rescued targets. Days 4-6: the oracle-information bound. ADF runs a team in one JVM, so give AIT a static shared WorldInfo: instant perfect sharing, same decision logic. Run it on the same 60 cases. KILL if the oracle gain is under 8% relative score on at least 3 of 4 maps in the degraded profiles, or if under full comms fewer than 10% of radio bytes are discarded and median information latency is under 5 steps.
candidates.key_risks: (1) Headroom may be small. AIT's design deliberately relies on platoon autonomy and zone partitioning, and the score may be limited by blockade and fire physics rather than information. The oracle pilot decides this. (2) Community size and credibility: only 3 teams in the 2025 final, and I found no 2026 results on the league site. Some ML reviewers will not know RCRS, and 'SOTA among RoboCup teams' may be discounted. Mitigations: also enter the RoboCup 2027 competition, and report against max-sum/DCOP. (3) Without Timrad's binaries the claim is only 'beats the 2024 champion and the 2025 runner-up'. (4) Steps are wall-clock timed, so CPU contention changes outcomes. Cap parallelism, audit missed commands per team, use paired seeds, and expect nondeterminism (this echoes the CBJA memory note on quiet-host measurement). (5) The hazard models may not transfer to unseen maps; leave-one-map-out is mandatory. (6) About 6 weeks of Java/ADF engineering. The Python CBJA engine is not reusable. (7) Reviewers may call packing and deduplication engineering; the ablations must show that the value x staleness pricing adds beyond them.
candidates.closest_prior_work: AIT-Rescue distributed-control strategy (Ando et al., LNCS 2025): static-priority messaging and autonomy. Bedi, Zhang, Chabot, 'Information-Driven Team Collaboration in RoboCup Rescue', Information 2025 (doi 10.3390/info17010008): task model plus communication protocol, +12-48% over the default sample agents only. Fujii et al., 'Distributed Operation of Binary Max-Sum with Coordination Variables in RoboCupRescue', IIAI Letters 2026. RMASBench (Kleiner et al., AAMAS 2013) and max-sum in RoboCup Rescue (Ramchurn et al., Computer Journal 2010). AC-DMTA (Drones 2026): stale records as interval bids. CBBA with Relays (Ponda et al., JSAC 2012). MARL message valuation: Shapley Message Value (IJCAI 2022) and Dynamic Size Message Scheduling under limited bandwidth (IEEE TMC 2024). CBJA (VOC selection). Novelty check: Crossref and arXiv searches for RoboCup Rescue coordination, age-of-information task allocation and stale-information CBBA found nothing that does value x staleness pricing for team-level shared-channel arbitration and targeting in RCRS. The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so this check is not exhaustive.
candidates.problem_formulation: A heterogeneous team (fire brigades, police forces, ambulance teams, plus centres) acts in a partially observable, stochastic city: fires spread, civilians' HP decays (stochastic deadlines), and blockades gate movement. At each step t, agent i observes its line of sight and may send on voice (30 m, 1 message of at most 256 B) and on one radio channel whose per-step capacity B_c is shared by the whole team, with profile-specific failure and dropout. Decisions: (a) a send set S_i,t that maximizes team value of information subject to sum over i of bytes(S_i,t) <= B_c (enforced implicitly via a common price); (b) a target action in {hold, verify, switch-to-k, defer}. Objective: the official RSL21 score at the final step.
candidates.reuse_from_cbja: The statistics and campaign methodology: paired bootstrap, Holm, TOST, prespecified confirmation blocks (scripts/analyze_v5.py, analyze_v10_confirm.py, docs/v10-confirmation-plan.md) and the resumable ProcessPool campaign runner, adapted to launch docker runs. The lesson of pricing per new item rather than per message, which becomes per-byte team pricing plus designated reporters. The measured fact that notice propagation dominated severe-link violations. The Gilbert-Elliott and relay knowledge, used to design store-carry-forward. Host notes on CPU quota and quiet-host measurement. Not reused: the Python engine, the CBJA allocators, and the Kev judges. The System-1 role is taken by tiny tabular hazard models.
candidates.evaluation_protocol: Prespecified before running. 11 maps x 6 official profiles x 20 paired seeds, for AIT-2024, AIT+FRESH, the 2 simple-rule variants, the ADF sample team, and the DCOP module (plus Timrad and 3Rakshak binaries if obtained). Hazards are trained on 6 development maps; the headline is on 5 held-out maps, as in a competition with unseen maps. Primary contrast: mean paired relative score gain of FRESH over AIT across the four degraded profiles (midle, low, fullJammer, noneChannel), with bootstrap 95% CI and Holm correction across profiles. Secondary: non-inferiority (-1% margin, TOST) on full and high, and the mechanism metrics (bytes discarded, information latency, wasted trips). Then a confirmation block on fresh seeds. Fixed concurrency and core pinning, with a missed-command audit for every team.
candidates.compute_and_timeline: CPU-bound; GPUs are not needed except optionally for hazard-model training. About 48 runs/hour at 8 concurrent runs on 96 cores. Week 1: pilot (60 + 60 runs). Weeks 2-3: log about 3k training runs and train the hazards (about 2.5 days of runs). Weeks 3-8: Java ADF modules plus ablations. Weeks 9-10: main campaign of about 7.9k runs (about 7 days). Weeks 11-12: confirmation block and writing. About 3 months in total.
