candidates.name: QUIET: zero-message replicated bundle allocation with evidence-age tracking on PARTNR's decentralized track
candidates.one_line: PARTNR's official decentralized track has no communication channel (verified in the partnr-planner README). Both agents run the same fine-tuned System-1 parser on the shared instruction and known house layout to get a symbolic goal graph. They then run the same deterministic CBBA-equivalent bundle allocation, so they agree on who does what without any messages. Divergence from private observations is priced by evidence age: hold, re-observe, take over or defer.
candidates.arena: PARTNR (Chang et al., ICLR 2025), a two-agent heterogeneous household task benchmark with spatial, temporal and capability constraints in Habitat 3.0. Code: github.com/facebookresearch/partnr-planner (MIT, cloned). Episodes: huggingface ai-habitat/partnr_episodes (CC BY-NC 4.0). Verified on the HF file listing: splits are train (about 100k), train_132k_unverified, train_2k, val (about 1k episodes) and val_mini, and NO public test split. Headline track: decentralized, partial observability (layout and furniture known, objects unknown), oracle skills. Secondary track: learned skills. Metrics: success rate (SR) and percent complete from the official evaluation functions, sim steps, planning cycles or LLM calls, and wall-clock time. Evaluation is on the full val split, with every baseline re-run from the official configs; the paper's test-set Table 2 is reported for context.
candidates.algorithm: (1) System-1 goal parser. LoRA fine-tune Qwen3-4B/8B or the researcher's Kev-4B, with grammar-constrained decoding into PARTNR's proposition and constraint language: is_on_top, is_inside, is_next_to, is_clean, is_filled, is_powered_on, plus temporal ordering, same- and different-argument constraints, and capability tags for human-only actions. Input: instruction plus static layout (rooms, furniture, receptacles), which both agents know under partial observability. Supervision: the train split's evaluation functions, 100k exact targets. Greedy deterministic decoding gives both agents the identical graph with no messages. (2) Replicated allocation. A CBBA-equivalent sequential-greedy bundle auction, or an exact tiny MILP since episodes have about 12 subtasks or fewer. Subtasks are find(object class), pick-place and state-change, with capability masks and precedence. It uses only public inputs (the graph, the layout, and agent start positions if the track exposes them; otherwise a deterministic room partition with id tie-breaks). Exploration is allocated as coverage bundles over furniture. Output: my ordered bundle plus a predicted schedule for the partner. (3) Evidence-age tracking, i.e. hold / ask again / defer under zero bandwidth. The belief over each subtask's status and each object's location carries timestamps. Partner progress is predicted from the replicated schedule, using a small regressor of completion times trained on train rollouts, and is updated by any partner-caused world-graph change the agent observes. Each decision picks one of: HOLD (continue own bundle); VERIFY (navigate to re-observe a stale, decision-relevant place, priced as travel cost versus expected loss from acting on a wrong belief); TAKE-OVER (a partner subtask whose predicted P(done by horizon) is low); DEFER (skip an own subtask that the evidence says the partner already did). After a surprise, re-allocation uses only facts both agents can infer, so the replicas stay consistent; private facts only reorder the agent's own bundle. (4) Execution uses PARTNR's oracle skill tools (Navigate, Explore, Pick, Place, Open/Close, Clean, Fill, PowerOn/Off).
candidates.why_it_should_win: PARTNR's own analysis (published test numbers) makes the case. Decentralized ReAct with Llama-3.1-70B reaches SR 0.73 at 3,295 sim steps, centralized ReAct 0.74 at 2,298, and the privileged heuristic expert 0.84 at 1,261; humans reach 0.93. The paper reports about 300% extraneous effort in decentralized settings, and task-tracking failures (steps not completed, wrong order, completed steps undone). Replicated allocation removes duplicate and conflicting effort by construction, with zero messages. Adding a dialogue channel does not solve this: it cut conflicts by 40-83 points but lowered success (Dongre & Hakkani-Tür, 2026). The parser attacks the SR-limiting failure directly. PARTNR's instructions are LLM-generated, which is the regime where the researcher's fine-tuned small judges reached .98-.99 on unseen model-written text; the real-notice collapse does not apply here. Executing against an explicit goal graph eliminates 'forgot a step' and 'undid a step'. Target on the full val split: SR >= 0.80 (vs about 0.73 for decentralized ReAct-70B, re-run), sim steps <= 2,200 (-33%), and one small-model parse per episode instead of about 15 LLM planning cycles per agent. With about 1,000 paired episodes, the standard error of a paired SR difference is about 1.5 points, so +6 points is well beyond noise.
candidates.baselines_to_beat: Official partnr-planner baselines, all re-run on val. Published test numbers (Table 2, verified from the arXiv HTML): decentralized zero-shot ReAct (Llama-3.1-70B) 0.73 SR / 0.86 PC / 3,295 steps / 15.24 cycles; centralized ReAct, partial obs, 0.74 / 2,298 steps; fine-tuned 8B planner 0.70 / 3,229 / 12.85; heuristic expert (privileged, full obs) 0.84 / 1,261; learned skills 0.57; learned skills plus ConceptGraphs 0.30. Also re-run the strongest open reasoning LLM that fits 4x H100 as a decentralized ReAct planner, since arXiv 2507.06157 reports o3-mini beating GPT-4o and Llama in every PARTNR setting (numbers not extracted). Later methods: LLawCo (ICML 2026; PARTNR-Dialog 74-75% SR; a different track with messaging; code release unverified); FLEET (arXiv 2510.07417; LLM to task graph to centralized MILP; 0.59 on its own 2-agent subset; no code).
candidates.cbja_failure_mode_check: Infrastructure parity: every method gets the same oracle skills, perception and world graph. QUIET gets no extra observations and sends no messages, so it complies with the track. Collapse check: pre-register the simple alternatives, i.e. no allocation (each agent does every subtask it can), a static split by agent id, 'always verify' and 'never verify'. Log how often evidence-age pricing picks a different action from the better rule, and drop the tracker if that happens on fewer than 5% of decisions. Attribution: ablate parser plus ReAct execution, parser plus replicated allocation, and the full method, so an SR gain that really comes from goal parsing is reported as such and not credited to coordination. Headroom is real and external: 11 SR points and about 2,000 steps separate the best decentralized planner from the privileged heuristic.
candidates.cheap_pilot: Days 1-2: install partnr-planner and the HSSD and episode data, then reproduce decentralized ReAct (Llama-3.1-8B, and 70B via vLLM with tensor parallelism 4) on 200 val episodes, matching the paper within CI. Days 2-3: LoRA fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B on train goal graphs (about 4 H100-hours) and measure exact match and proposition F1 on val. Days 4-6: implement replicated greedy allocation plus an oracle-skill executor (no tracking yet) and run it on the same 200 episodes. KILL if parser proposition F1 is below 0.90, if pilot SR is below the reproduced ReAct-70B SR, or if the sim-step reduction is under 20%.
candidates.key_risks: (1) Only two agents. Allocation headroom is limited, and MRTA reviewers may not count PARTNR as multi-robot task allocation. Centralized ReAct beats decentralized by just 1 SR point, so most of the SR gain may come from the parser, not from coordination, and the allocation's main contribution may be efficiency (steps). (2) The test split is hidden, so results are on val with every baseline re-run; reviewers may ask why the published test numbers are not matched. (3) The critique that the parser 'learns the grader format', and doubts about generalization beyond LLM-written instructions. Mitigate with the learned-skills track and held-out scenes. (4) The deterministic replicas can diverge when observations differ; the 'public facts only' re-allocation may be too conservative. (5) Scoop risk: PARTNR is active (LLawCo at ICML 2026, dialogue alignment 2026, CoBel-World), and reasoning-model baselines may already exceed 0.73. (6) Habitat 3.0 setup and GPU rendering cost. (7) Dataset licence is CC BY-NC (research use only). (8) There is no degraded-link component, so PARTNR is the zero-bandwidth extreme rather than a lossy channel.
candidates.closest_prior_work: PARTNR baselines, including its fine-tuned 8B planner (arXiv 2411.00081). LLawCo (arXiv 2606.28182, ICML 2026; PARTNR-Dialog, messaging track). Dongre & Hakkani-Tür, 'Embodied Multi-Agent Coordination by Aligning World Models Through Dialogue' (arXiv 2605.12920): dialogue reduces conflicts but hurts success. 'Evaluation of Habitat Robotics using LLMs' (arXiv 2507.06157). FLEET (arXiv 2510.07417): language to task graph to MILP, centralized. CoBel-World (arXiv 2509.21981): belief-driven communication on TDW-MAT and C-WAH. LaMMA-P (ICRA 2025): language to PDDL. From MRTA: DMCHBA and HIPC (replicated or implicit planning) and FORMICA (arXiv 2602.18622, communication-free teammate-bid prediction). An arXiv abstract search for 'PARTNR' returned only 5 papers, and none proposes communication-free replicated allocation on the official decentralized track. The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so this check is not exhaustive.
candidates.problem_formulation: A two-agent Dec-POMDP with no communication channel. Shared inputs: instruction I and static layout L. Private observations o_i,t. The goal G(I,L) is a conjunction of propositions with temporal, argument and capability constraints, checked by the official evaluation function. Each agent picks skills from a shared library. Objective: maximize P(G satisfied) within the step budget and minimize sim steps. The structure: G_hat = f_theta(I, L) (System-1), then a replicated allocation pi = A(G_hat, L, public facts), then a per-agent tracking policy over {hold, verify, take-over, defer} under evidence age.
candidates.reuse_from_cbja: The Kev/LoRA fine-tuning pipeline and configs (runs/kev-ft), the zoo and vLLM serving with the pointer head (serving/zoo_server.py, serving/vllm_backend.py), constrained decoding, and judge-answer caching. The atomic design in which language produces atoms and code composes the decision (cbja/atomic.py) maps directly to instruction, then propositions, then code-composed plan. The paired-statistics and confirmation-block workflow. The CBJA findings that fine-tuning the small model mattered more than clever query selection, and that the no-text shortcut paid off, which becomes one parse per episode instead of per-step LLM calls.
candidates.evaluation_protocol: Full val split (about 1k episodes), paired across methods on identical episodes and seeds. Primary: SR difference of QUIET minus the best re-run decentralized baseline, with bootstrap 95% CI. Secondary: sim steps (-33% target), percent complete, number of LLM calls, wall-clock time, and the learned-skills track. Pre-registered ablations: parser plus ReAct, parser plus no-allocation, parser plus static split, and the always/never-verify rules. Pre-register the analysis on val_mini and the 2k development subset, then run val once as the confirmation block.
candidates.compute_and_timeline: GPU-heavy. Parser fine-tuning takes about 1-2 H100-days. Baseline re-runs with 70B-class LLMs on 4x H100 plus Habitat evaluation of about 1k episodes x 6-8 methods take about 1-2 days per method. Week 1: pilot. Weeks 2-4: full parser and tracker. Weeks 5-7: baselines and ablations. Weeks 8-9: val confirmation and writing. About 2-2.5 months in total.
candidates.target_venue: ICML 2027 or CoRL 2027, with AAMAS 2028 as the multi-agent-venue alternative.

candidates.name: C3-PARTNR: Compile once, commit from common knowledge (silent decentralized execution of compiled goals)
candidates.one_line: On PARTNR's official decentralized, partial-observability track, the per-step LLM ReAct loop is replaced. A small fine-tuned model compiles the instruction once into PARTNR's own proposition and constraint program. Each agent executes that program through the same deterministic joint scheduler, which uses only common knowledge and sends no messages, plus a learned object-placement search prior. A slow LLM is called only when the compile is uncertain or execution stalls.
candidates.arena: PARTNR (ICLR 2025, Meta). Code is MIT at github.com/facebookresearch/partnr-planner; episodes are CC-BY-NC on HF ai-habitat/partnr_episodes. Official track: decentralized planners (the README states there is no explicit communication between them), partial observability (layout known, object locations unknown), oracle skills. Evaluation is on the public 1,000-episode val split, whose released file has 12 scene ids against 13 in the paper, all unseen in train. The test split is not released (HF README lists train_132k_unverified, train=111,652 HITL-verified, train_2k, train_mini, val, val_mini), so ask Meta to evaluate on test. Primary endpoint: success rate (SR). Co-primary efficiency endpoint: simulator steps. Secondary: percent complete (PC), planning cycles and slow-LLM calls, tokens, wall-clock, per-category SR (constraint-free, spatial, temporal, heterogeneous), and the learned-skill track (ReAct 0.57 SR, 6,495 steps).
candidates.problem_formulation: Two heterogeneous agents, a Spot robot and a humanoid. Only the humanoid can perform clean, fill and power on/off. They receive one NL instruction. Each agent keeps a private world graph: rooms and furniture are common knowledge at t=0, objects are discovered by exploration. Success means PARTNR's evaluation function holds at the end: propositions (is_on_top, is_inside, is_next_to, is_in_room, is_clean, is_filled, is_powered_on/off, is_on_floor) under Temporal, Terminal, SameArg and DifferentArg constraints. Measured on the released val file this session: 4.1 propositions per episode on average (max 26), 265/1,000 episodes with temporal DAG edges, 222/1,000 with human-only predicates, 4-7 rigid objects typical. Minimize simulator steps subject to success, with no inter-agent messages (official decentralized protocol).
candidates.algorithm: (1) Goal compiler (System-1). Fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B or 4B (LoRA; the CBJA Kev fine-tune and serving stack can be reused) on the 111,652 train episodes. Input: instruction plus the furniture and room list, all common knowledge. Output: a lifted program in PARTNR's evaluation DSL. Object handles are replaced by category and attribute descriptors (derived automatically from episode metadata); furniture handles are grounded directly because the layout is known. Constraints are emitted as a DAG. Grammar-constrained greedy decoding, so both agents produce the identical program from identical input. k=5 samples are drawn to estimate confidence. If the samples disagree semantically, one slow-LLM call (e.g., Qwen3-235B-A22B on local vLLM) adjudicates among the candidate programs. (2) Belief-level proposition checker. Each agent evaluates every compiled proposition on its own world graph as satisfied, unsatisfied or unknown, and enforces terminal and temporal constraints (never undo a satisfied terminal proposition). This replaces LLM task tracking. (3) Common-knowledge joint scheduler, replicated deterministically on both agents. It solves the tiny joint problem exactly by DP or brute force (at most 26 propositions, usually 4) over the remaining propositions. Inputs: capabilities (human-only predicates go to the humanoid), temporal DAG, travel costs from the known layout, and expected search cost for undiscovered objects. Inputs are restricted to common knowledge (initial poses, compiled program, layout) plus a shared duration model, so both agents predict the same joint plan and the partner's progress without messages, in the HIPC and MACKRL spirit. Private discoveries enter only through commitments the partner can infer. If an agent observes that a proposition assigned to its partner became satisfied, or that its own target is taken, it replans with a fixed tie-break (CBBA-style: lower expected completion time wins, agent id breaks ties). (4) Search partition plus System-1 placement prior. A small classifier P(furniture or room | object category), trained on train-episode initial placements, orders exploration. Furniture is split deterministically between the agents by the replicated scheduler, so the two never search the same place. (5) Slow-LLM escalation triggers only on compile disagreement, two consecutive skill failures on the same subgoal, or no proposition progress within T steps. This is a plain rule and is not claimed as novel. (6) Protocol hygiene: evaluation_* fields are stripped from episodes before agent code sees them, verified by an audit test.
candidates.why_it_should_win: The PARTNR authors name the dominant LLM failures as task tracking (not completing all steps, wrong order, undoing completed steps) and poor tracking of partner actions. Decentralized ReAct needs 3,295 steps against 1,261 for the privileged Heuristic-Expert. In the o3-mini/GPT-4o study, decentralized partial observability is where steps explode: 4,977 for o3-mini and 5,375 for GPT-4o. Temporal tasks lose 27% and heterogeneous tasks lose 20% relative to constraint-free ones. Each of these has a structural fix. Tracking: the compiled proposition checker is exact on the agent's belief. Order and capability: the constraint DAG plus capability-aware exact scheduling. Duplicate work and duplicate search: replicated common-knowledge assignment and a deterministic search partition, with no messages. The dialogue study (2605.12920) found silent coordination beats LLM dialogue on PARTNR, which supports a message-free design. The Heuristic-Expert shows the achievable bound given a correct spec: 0.84 SR at 1,261 steps with full observability. Centralized ReAct goes from 1,347 steps (full) to 2,298 (partial), so exploration costs about 1,000 steps. A correct compile plus good search should therefore land near SR 0.80-0.84 at about 1,800-2,300 steps, with about 0.1-0.3 slow-LLM calls per episode instead of 9-15 planning cycles. Episodes are paired and n=1,000: a +7 pt SR gap has a paired SE of about 1.3-1.5 pt, so it is significant at more than 4 SE. The step and LLM-call reductions are far larger than noise.
candidates.baselines_to_beat: All from partnr-planner (MIT; decentralized partial observability, oracle skills, 1,000 episodes) unless noted. ReAct Llama-3.1-70B: SR 0.73, PC 0.86, 3,295 steps, 15.24 planning cycles. ReAct-RAG: 0.71, 3,467 steps. Fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B planner: 0.70, 3,229 steps, 12.85 cycles, 8.6x faster inference. Centralized ReAct with partial observability: 0.74, 2,298 steps. Heuristic-Expert (privileged, full observability, reads the evaluation function; a reference ceiling, not a baseline): 0.84, 1,261 steps. Humans: 0.93. Learned-skill track: ReAct 0.57, 6,495 steps; with ConceptGraphs 0.30. Frontier backbones, decentralized partial observability (arXiv 2507.06157, small n, about 10 h per model): o3-mini SR 0.77, PC 0.92, 4,977 steps; GPT-4o 0.73, 5,375 steps. LLawCo (ICML 2026) on PARTNR-Dialog (val, with a talk channel, a different track; code release unverified): Llama-3.1-70B 0.75, 2,526.5 steps; Qwen3-14B 0.74, 2,131.8 steps. FLEET (arXiv 2510.07417, no code, a PARTNR subset in a non-comparable setting): 0.59 vs 0.28. The real bar we must run ourselves on the full val set: ReAct with a frontier open-weight reasoning backbone (Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking or gpt-oss-120b on 4x H100), plus ReAct given our compiled checklist and search prior as tools (equal infrastructure).
candidates.cbja_failure_mode_check: Why this is not the CBJA collapse. CBJA's novelty was a selector whose decisions matched a deadline rule in 98.6-98.9% of cases, evaluated on a self-built testbed. Here the claim is system-level, on an external benchmark with MIT baseline code and 1,000 paired episodes, and the architecture differs from ReAct at every step. The gain decomposes into measurable parts, each with an ablation: compiler vs few-shot LLM compile, proposition checker, replicated scheduler vs greedy nearest-claim, search partition, placement prior, and escalation. The oracle-spec upper bound separates compile error from execution error. Brutal part: with 2 agents and about 4 propositions, the allocator itself will very likely be rule-equivalent. Greedy nearest-claim with capability and temporal checks may match the exact replicated schedule. We will log how often the two disagree, report it, and not claim allocator novelty if it is under 5%. The novelty then rests on compile-once plus silent common-knowledge coordination with a search partition. The escalation trigger is a threshold rule by design, so no VOC. Largest collapse risk: ReAct given the compiled checklist and prior as tools (equal infrastructure, per the CBJA lesson) could close most of the gap. The paper then becomes 'compiled goals fix LLM planners'. That is still a SOTA result, but a smaller contribution.
candidates.cheap_pilot: Five working days, about 3 GPU-days. Day 1-2: install Habitat and partnr-planner on an H100 with headless EGL. Reproduce the Heuristic-Expert and ReAct-8B on val_mini (369 episodes); they should match the paper within CI. Day 2-4, in parallel: (a) Fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B as compiler on train and measure execution-equivalent program accuracy on val (a program counts as correct if evaluated against the ground-truth final state it matches the ground-truth evaluation function). (b) Oracle-spec pilot: feed the ground-truth evaluation function (privileged, pilot only) to the replicated scheduler, search partition and uniform search prior, then run 300 val episodes decentralized with partial observability. Kill criteria: oracle-spec SR below 0.80 or mean steps above 2,300 (execution cannot beat the bar), or compiler equivalence below 0.88, since the product of the two bounds achievable SR. Day 5: run ReAct-70B plus the compiled-checklist tool on 200 episodes. If it comes within 3 pt SR and 15% steps of the oracle-spec pilot, the multi-agent layer is not the story; pivot the framing or drop the candidate.
candidates.key_risks: (1) The SR margin may be small against a frontier reasoning backbone we re-run. o3-mini already reaches 0.77 (small n), the privileged ceiling is 0.84 and humans reach 0.93, so SOTA may rest mainly on efficiency: steps -35 to -55% and LLM calls -90%. That is defensible because PARTNR reports steps as a first-class metric, but it is weaker than a clean SR win. (2) Novelty critique: instruction-to-formal-goal plus symbolic execution already exists for single-agent PARTNR (AHAT/TGPO: 82.6% on a text-only, single-agent PARTNR planning setting), for centralized teams (FLEET) and for MAT-THOR (LaMMA-P). The multi-agent contribution (silent common-knowledge scheduling) is thin at N=2 and 4 propositions. (3) Learning the labeler: PARTNR instructions and evaluation functions are LLM-generated and HITL-filtered. A compiler trained on them may exploit generator regularities. Report a no-fine-tune few-shot compiler variant and state data provenance honestly (CBJA lesson). (4) No public test split: val is shared by everyone, including LLawCo. Limit tuning to train-scene dev sets and prespecify one confirmation run. (5) Habitat install and rendering on this box; oracle-skill failures cap SR. (6) The steps target overlaps LLawCo's 2,131 steps (Qwen3-14B, with a talk channel on a different track), so the efficiency margin over that line may be modest. (7) Meta or LLawCo follow-ups could publish a similar structured planner first. The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so novelty was checked through 90 Semantic Scholar citers of PARTNR plus arXiv search pages, which is not exhaustive.
candidates.closest_prior_work: All verified this session unless noted. FLEET (arXiv 2510.07417, no venue, no code): LLM to task graph plus fitness matrix plus centralized MILP scheduling; on a PARTNR subset 0.59 vs 0.28. AHAT/TGPO (arXiv 2602.12244): Qwen2.5-7B maps instruction plus scene graph to PDDL subgoals; 82.6% on text-only single-agent PARTNR planning vs SayPlan 72.2%. LaMMA-P (ICRA 2025): LLM to PDDL for multi-robot teams on MAT-THOR. LLawCo (ICML 2026) and PARTNR-Dialog. 'Embodied Multi-Agent Coordination by Aligning World Models Through Dialogue' (arXiv 2605.12920, SIGDIAL 2026): dialogue cuts conflicts 40-83 pts but lowers success vs silent coordination. PARTNR's own fine-tuned planner and Heuristic-Expert. Evaluation of Habitat Robotics using LLMs (arXiv 2507.06157). Implicit coordination from shared information: HIPC and DMCHBA in MRTA, MACKRL (NeurIPS 2019). BRACE (arXiv 2608.01428): rule-gated budgeted replanning, but single-agent Habitat PointNav. Among the 90 Semantic Scholar citers of PARTNR, none reports compile-then-execute with silent replicated scheduling on the official decentralized partial-observability track. WebSearch was unavailable, so this check is not exhaustive.
candidates.evaluation_protocol: Prespecified before any val run. Endpoint 1: SR vs ReAct-70B and vs the re-run frontier-backbone ReAct, by paired McNemar test plus paired bootstrap. Endpoint 2: paired log step ratio. Holm correction across the two families. Tune only on train-scene dev episodes, then run a single confirmation on val (1,000 episodes, 3 seeds for stochastic components). Report per-category SR, PC, slow-LLM calls, tokens and wall-clock. Report the ablation ladder: oracle-spec, −prior, −partition, greedy-claim, LLM-compile, ReAct+tools. Report the learned-skill track as secondary. Ask Meta for a test-split run. An audit test proves the agents never read evaluation_* fields.
candidates.compute_and_timeline: Compiler fine-tune: 4-8 H100-hours per model. Habitat plus oracle skills: about 1-3 min per episode, so 1,000 episodes x about 10 configurations take 1-2 days on 4 GPUs and 96 cores. The 70B and 235B baselines on local vLLM need about 30k calls per full val run. Timeline: week 1 setup and pilot, weeks 2-6 method, weeks 7-8 baselines and prespecified confirmation, weeks 9-10 writing.
candidates.reuse_from_cbja: Kev/Qwen3 LoRA fine-tuning and vLLM/zoo serving (runs/kev-ft scripts, serving/zoo_server.py, serving/vllm_backend.py) for the compiler and prior. The atomic-pipeline design idea (language to atoms, code composes the decision) becomes language to propositions, with code doing the tracking. The no-text-shortcut lesson becomes: skip the slow LLM whenever the compile is confident. The paired bootstrap, Holm, TOST and prespecified-confirmation workflow (scripts/analyze_v5.py, analyze_v10_confirm.py) and the resumable parallel runner. Lessons applied: give baselines equal infrastructure, log decision divergence against the simple rule, never report model-written text as author-written.
candidates.target_venue: ICML 2027 (late Jan 2027) or RSS 2027; CoRL 2027 as fallback. An ICLR 2027 submission is too early.

candidates.name: FPCC-Wildfire: Forecast-priced coalition consensus on CREW-Wildfire
candidates.one_line: A decentralized CBBA with time windows and coalitions, whose tasks and bids come from a small learned System-1 fire forecaster. The forecaster infers the hidden wind, moisture and slope fields from observed spread and prices each firebreak segment, rescue and helicopter transport by the burned-area loss it avoids before the forecast arrival deadline. The LLM only compiles the mission text and handles out-of-spec events. Target: the dynamic levels where every published LLM multi-agent framework scores below Do-Nothing.
candidates.arena: CREW-Wildfire (Hyun, Waytowich, Chen; arXiv 2507.05178; Semantic Scholar lists the venue as TMLR). Code at github.com/generalroboticslab/CREW-Wildfire, Apache-2.0 LICENSE, verified. Unity (Dojo) plus Python, with official implementations of CAMON, COELA, Embodied and HMAS-2. 17 official level configurations with 3-15 heterogeneous agents: firefighters, bulldozers, drones, helicopters. The SOTA claim is on the 9 unsaturated configurations: Suppress Fire Extinguish, Contain, Locate+Suppress and Locate+Deploy+Suppress; Full Game; Rescue Known-Location (Large); Search and Rescue; Search+Rescue+Transport; Scout Fire (Large). The Cut-Trees and Transport levels are already near max, so there we only report parity. Metrics: the official score per level; normalized gap closure (score − DoNothing)/(max − DoNothing); API calls and tokens.
candidates.problem_formulation: The fire model is a cellular automaton. Verified in MapManager.cs: spread is deterministic via thresholds on a Ratio built from slope factor, moisture, wetness and wind alignment. The wind, moisture and elevation fields are Perlin-noise maps hidden from agents, which observe only local cell-state grids of 21x21 (ground units), 51x51 (drones) and 61x61 (helicopters). Decisions are made every 10 frames, step-synchronously (the simulation waits for the policy). Penalty levels score −(trees destroyed + 20 x agents lost). Finite levels count civilians rescued, fire located, and so on. Message passing is broadcast and lossless. Objective: maximize the official score. Decentralized: each agent decides from its own observations plus received messages.
candidates.algorithm: (1) Mission compile: one LLM call per episode (local Qwen3-32B) maps task_description to objective weights and allowed task types; re-invoked only on out-of-spec events. (2) System-1 hidden-field forecaster. A ConvGRU or U-Net of about 5-20M params, under 20 ms on CPU. Input: the fused team observation history (cell states, vegetation). Output: per-cell ignition-time quantiles over H decision steps. It implicitly infers wind, moisture and slope from the observed front. Trained on millions of rollouts from a bit-exact JAX port of MapManager.cs (Simulate, Ratio, SlopeFactor), whose trace parity with the Unity build is checked. A second, amortized head predicts the counterfactual burned-area reduction of cutting segment s by time t. Its training labels are exact rollouts of the port with s removed. (3) Task generation. Candidate containment contours are closed low-cost cuts on the grid, with cells feasible only where forecast arrival (quantile q) exceeds estimated crew completion time; each contour is split into segments. Also generated: civilian rescues with deadline = forecast arrival at the civilian, helicopter transports as coalition tasks (helicopter + k firefighters, pickup before drop-off), drone scouting cells from a coverage prior, and extinguish tasks where water exists. (4) Consensus allocation. CBBA with time windows, keeping per-task winner, bid and timestamp tables. Implementation follows Choi 2009, not CBJA's row fusion. Bids = forecast-priced marginal loss reduction within the deadline. A CBGA-style coalition extension handles the transport and firefighter bundles. Rebroadcast is event-triggered when forecast quantiles shift more than δ (ED-CBBA style). (5) Forecast safety shield: never occupy cells whose arrival quantile is below travel time plus margin. This removes the x20 agent-loss penalty. The shield is also given to every baseline. (6) Scouting uses the simple incremental deadline and coverage rule, not VOC, because of the CBJA lesson.
candidates.why_it_should_win: The published LLM frameworks fail in exactly the regime this method targets. Verified from Table 3 of the paper: on all four Suppress Fire levels and the Full Game every LLM framework scores at or below Do-Nothing (e.g., Contain: CAMON −736.67 vs Do-Nothing −660.67; Extinguish −593.33 vs −519.67). On Locate+Suppress (−1,062.67) and Locate+Deploy+Suppress (−729.67) all four frameworks equal Do-Nothing, so they never act usefully. Search and Rescue and Search+Rescue+Transport score 0 for every framework. The paper's own failure analysis cites overlapping actions, failed decomposition, and agents persisting in outdated plans. The mechanistic reasons: (a) an LLM sees a 21x21 ASCII window and emits one primitive per decision. It cannot integrate anisotropic, slope- and wind-driven front dynamics over a 60-200-cell map. The CA is deterministic given hidden fields, so a learned inverse model plus forward rollout gives accurate arrival times. (b) Containment is a deadline race: a break line only helps if finished before arrival. That is exactly CBBA with time windows, and the counterfactual-value bids direct scarce crews (5 firefighters and 1 bulldozer on a 60x60 map) to segments with the largest avoided loss. (c) Agent deaths cost 20 each, and a forecast shield removes them. (d) Coupled tasks (helicopter transport, drone scouting feeding ground crews) are coalition and precedence structures that consensus auctions handle and free-text dialogue does not. Expected margins (hypotheses to be falsified by the pilot): at least 50% gap closure on Contain and Extinguish, positive gains on the Locate levels, at least 3/5 civilians on Search and Rescue, with 1-2 orders of magnitude fewer LLM tokens.
candidates.baselines_to_beat: Published (GPT-4o, 3-10 seeds, Table 3 of 2507.05178). Suppress Extinguish: CAMON −593.33, COELA −635.00, Embodied −636.33, HMAS-2 −624.33, Do-Nothing −519.67. Contain: −736.67 / −751.33 / −757.33 / −739.00, Do-Nothing −660.67. Locate+Suppress: all −1,062.67 (= Do-Nothing). Locate+Deploy+Suppress: all −729.67 (= Do-Nothing). Full Game: best COELA −5,516.00 vs Do-Nothing −5,502.67. Rescue Known Large: best Embodied 4.33/9. Search and Rescue: 0/5 for all. Search+Rescue+Transport: 0/10 for all. Scout Fire Large: 0/2 for all. Saturated levels, parity only: CAMON 18/18, 72/75, 30/30, 94.33/105, 6/6, 10/12. Official code for all four frameworks is in the repo (Apache-2.0). We re-run them with one open-weight backbone on the same seeds and also cite the GPT-4o numbers. Required strong non-LLM baselines, self-implemented and flagged as such: greedy nearest-fire plus shield; a fixed-radius or wind-skewed ring firebreak with Hungarian assignment; CBBA with distance bids and no forecast; the LLM frameworks given our forecast and shield as tools (equal infrastructure); and an oracle-hidden-map planner as an upper reference. Possible uncatalogued competitor: Khan et al., 'Beyond Single-Framework Architectures: A Systematic Evaluation and Hybrid Design for Scalable Multi-Agent Coordination' (IEEE Access 2026, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3683900). It cites CREW-Wildfire, but its abstract could not be retrieved this session, so read it before committing.
candidates.cbja_failure_mode_check: Beating the published numbers is nearly guaranteed and proves little, because the LLM frameworks lose to Do-Nothing. The real test is whether forecast pricing beats simple rules: the fixed-ring firebreak, and CBBA with distance bids plus the same safety shield. That is exactly where CBJA's VOC collapsed. Reasons it might not collapse: spread is strongly anisotropic, with wind fields in [−10, 10] per axis, slope factor exp(0.069·slope) and moisture scaling. Crews are capacity-limited, so an isotropic ring either wastes crew-time or is overrun, and counterfactual bids reorder segments in ways distance cannot. But this must be measured, not assumed. Log the fraction of decisions where FPCC and the ring or distance-CBBA rules differ. Prespecify the primary contrast as FPCC vs the best of {ring+Hungarian+shield, distance-CBBA+shield, LLM framework+forecast tools}. If the forecast-free shield baseline gets within 15% of FPCC's gap closure, the paper reduces to 'a safety rule beats LLM agents' and the candidate is dead. Scouting deliberately avoids VOC.
candidates.cheap_pilot: Five working days, CPU and GPU. Day 1-3: port MapManager.cs Simulate, Ratio and SlopeFactor, plus map generation, to NumPy/JAX. In parallel, attempt a headless Unity 2021.3 Linux server build of Wildfire and email the authors for a build. Verify cell-state trace parity on 20 seeds; if Unity cannot be built, parity is checked later, and the port alone must never be the reported benchmark. Day 3-5, in the port, 30 seeds each of Contain and Extinguish: Do-Nothing, greedy+shield, ring+Hungarian+shield, distance-CBBA+shield, and ORACLE-map forecast-priced CBBA (true hidden fields, which bounds FPCC). Kill criteria: the oracle method closes under 50% of the Do-Nothing loss; or its advantage over the best rule is under 15% of the Do-Nothing loss (forecasting would not matter); or no Unity build within about 2 weeks and no reply from the authors.
candidates.key_risks: (1) Engineering and adoption: no prebuilt binary. Per the docs, Unity Editor 2021.3 plus DojoBuilder, and possibly the Nakama/Docker stack, are needed. Headless Linux licensing and building may cost 1-2 weeks. (2) Benchmark credibility is moderate: one lab, 11 citers per Semantic Scholar, no non-LLM entries. Robotics and MRTA reviewers may see it as niche, and agentic-AI reviewers may call a mostly classical controller off-topic because the LLM contributes little. (3) Published baselines are weak, so the headline margin is trivially large. The scientific claim therefore rests on our self-implemented rule baselines, which is the CBJA self-baseline trap. Mitigate with equal infrastructure, prespecification and release of all baselines. (4) Deterministic CA: an oracle-map planner is near-optimal, so the method's value is exactly the hidden-field inference, which may be easy (smooth Perlin fields) or hard. Either way, a reviewer may call it simulator exploitation unless agents strictly use the official observation vector (enforce with an audit). (5) Published results use only 3-10 seeds with huge variance (±200-3,300). We will use 50 paired seeds, but the scores are not directly comparable to the paper's GPT-4o runs unless the frameworks are re-run. (6) Domain specificity: a 'wildfire controller' may not read as a general group-mission algorithm, so the CBBA-TW-coalition core must be shown to be generic. (7) Possible prior hybrid entry (Khan et al., IEEE Access 2026), not yet read.
candidates.closest_prior_work: CREW-Wildfire and its four LLM frameworks (CAMON, COELA, Embodied, HMAS-2). Boussioux, Jacquillat, Reger, Wachspress, 'Predictive and Prescriptive AI toward Optimizing Wildfire Suppression' (arXiv 2605.04510): ML spread estimation plus centralized integer optimization of crew assignment, with no decentralized or LLM component. CBBA (Choi, Brunet, How, T-RO 2009), CBGA coalition allocation (Hunt et al. 2014), chance-constrained CBBA (Ponda 2012), ED-CBBA (arXiv 2509.06481), and CC-OPI online deadline allocation (arXiv 2609.19208), all from the sweep. DynaHMRC (arXiv 2606.14882): LLM agents with leadership bidding. AeroWeaver (arXiv 2609.18520): LLM harness for UAV-swarm skill execution. Khan et al. (IEEE Access 2026): possibly a hybrid framework evaluated on CREW-Wildfire, unread. None of the 11 Semantic Scholar citers of CREW-Wildfire whose titles I could inspect is a non-LLM or forecast-driven method paper on it. The Khan et al. paper is the exception that must be checked.
candidates.evaluation_protocol: Official Unity build only for reported numbers; the JAX port is used only for training and the pilot. All 17 configurations, 50 paired seeds each (same seed means the same map for every method). Primary endpoint: mean normalized gap closure over the 9 unsaturated configurations, FPCC vs the best non-FPCC method, by paired bootstrap with Holm correction across levels. Secondary: per-level scores, agents lost, LLM calls and tokens. LLM frameworks are re-run with one open-weight backbone on 20 seeds per level, and the published GPT-4o numbers are also cited. Prespecified decision-divergence logging. A single confirmation block on fresh seeds.
candidates.compute_and_timeline: Forecaster and value-head training: 1-2 H100-days on JAX rollouts (about 1e6 episodes per hour on GPU). Unity evaluation: about 16-32 headless instances on 96 cores. LLM baselines: vLLM Qwen3-32B/70B on 2-4 H100s; 10-15 agents x hundreds of decisions per episode means about 1M calls, which takes days. Timeline: weeks 1-2 build, port and pilot; weeks 3-7 forecaster and CBBA-TW-coalition; weeks 8-9 full evaluation, baselines and confirmation; week 10 writing.
candidates.reuse_from_cbja: CBBA/SSI implementations as a behavioral reference only; they must be rewritten with canonical per-task winner, bid and timestamp tables. The incremental deadline-rule finding: use the rule for scouting and rebroadcast instead of VOC. Resumable parallel runner, paired bootstrap, Holm, TOST and the prespecified-confirmation workflow. Small-model serving for the mission compiler. Lessons applied: equal infrastructure, log divergence from the simple rule early, strong central and rule baselines.
candidates.target_venue: CoRL 2027 or IJCAI 2027; AAMAS 2028 as an alternative; TMLR as fallback, which matches the benchmark's own venue.

scores.rationale: This is the strongest candidate on evidence. I re-ran replay_check.py: 4 s single-core LNS scores 23.46 against RL(s.10) at 27.07, and replaying the plans in HeteroMRTA's own env gives exactly the same result. But the headline '13.4% over the published SOTA' is inflated. The shipped RALTestSet results.yaml files contain CTAS-D (600 s Gurobi), with a mean timeCost/100 of 23.67, which matches the paper's CTAS-D scale. My paired check (ac_ctasd_check.py) gives LNS/CTAS-D ratios of 1.000 [0.984, 1.014] at 4 s (25 of 50 wins) and 0.963 [0.948, 0.976] at 30 s (40 of 50 wins). So wherever the MILP finishes, the real margin over the best published method is about 0-4%, at 20-150x less compute. The large margins are only plausible on the AT and km=50 configurations where CTAS-D fails (0-40% success) and RL is the best published method; those are unmeasured, but their large waiting times suggest headroom. No newer paper reports on these sets: I checked all 42 Semantic Scholar citers of HeteroMRTA, and BAP (RA-L 2026) is min-max open VRP, not coalition scheduling. The gain does not collapse to a rule, since construction alone scores 29.7. The consensus layer, however, is only parallel seeds on static instances, which the authors admit. Novelty is therefore 'ALNS beats RL and a time-limited MILP', which is weak at AAMAS unless the decentralized-under-disturbance section is non-degenerate. Missing CBBA-lineage coalition baseline: CBTA (Wang et al., RA-L 2022, consensus timetable for simultaneous multi-agent tasks). Cheapest and most feasible path to a defensible benchmark SOTA.

Same arena and pilot as KOC-LNS, so the same CTAS-D caveat applies: the 12-16% target is against RL. The best published method where the MILP finishes is CTAS-D, which the 30 s LNS beats by only about 3.7% on RALTestSet. The prespecified endpoint (only vs RL(s.10) on the 4 largest configurations) would let a reviewer say CTAS-D at 18.65 on SA-BT kn=50/km=50 was ignored. Correct it to per-configuration min(CTAS-D, RL). The decentralized mechanism is the most genuinely CBBA-lineage and novel of the set: a key-order deadlock-freedom lemma, a max-plus timing CRDT, 2PC coalition commits with leases, and MGM-k arbitration. It is correctness-relevant rather than decorative, and it has good kill criteria (retain at least 70% of the centralized gain at p=0) plus TOST against centralized ALNS. Risks: much more engineering; on static instances a replicated same-seed ALNS ties it with zero messages, so its value shows only under delays or loss, which is partly a self-defined regime (mitigated by prespecified LoRR-style delays and CV_MRTA channel models). Closest CBBA-lineage prior art is now verified: CBTA (RA-L 2022; timetable consensus minimizing average start time; compared only with CBBA and CBGA) must be a baseline. Sync-VRP ALNS (Hojabri 2018) also weakens the novelty of the centralized core.

Same winnable arena, but the claimed contribution (a distilled student) is dominated by its own teacher at matched compute. A 4 s ALNS already ties CTAS-D and beats RL by 13%. A student within 5-8% of the teacher would beat RL by about 8-12%, but it would lose to plain ALNS run for the same total time. The authors' own collapse test (a 50 ms rolling ALNS) is likely to kill the learning claim. The headline '20% better under 30-50% loss' rests on a self-defined lossy extension with stale-state RL, which is the CBJA trap. 12+ weeks with DAgger relabelling and CBGA reimplementation; SADCHER already covers solver imitation for coalitions. Better used as a graft: an NDS-style learned destroy selector or warm start inside the LNS.

PARTNR is the most credible external benchmark in the set (ICLR 2025, Meta, MIT code, 1,000 val episodes). I verified the README: decentralized planners have 'no explicit communication', and there is no test split and no evaluation server, so every baseline must be re-run on val. The design is well hedged: an oracle-spec pilot, ReAct plus the same tools as an equal-infrastructure baseline, an evaluation-field audit, and a ladder of kill criteria. The most likely clear win is on efficiency (steps -35 to -55%, about 90% fewer LLM calls); an SR win is capped by the privileged 0.84 heuristic and by oracle-skill failures, and o3-mini is already at about 0.77 (arXiv 2507.06157; its abstract gives no numbers). Poor fit to the goal: 2 agents and about 4 propositions, and the authors admit the allocator will be rule-equivalent. Novelty sits on compile-then-execute (FLEET, AHAT/TGPO, LaMMA-P already exist). Habitat setup and 70B/235B baseline re-runs cost weeks. An MRTA or CBBA audience will not read this as group-mission SOTA.

The same PARTNR arena as C3-PARTNR, with a thinner protocol. Evidence-age hold/verify/take-over/defer at N=2 is likely to match a simple always- or never-verify rule, which is a CBJA-style collapse risk. The claim that fine-tuned small judges transfer comes from model-written text, and on real notices those judges scored .50-.72. As the authors admit, most of the SR gain would come from the parser, not from coordination. The target of SR >= 0.80 is optimistic given the 0.84 privileged ceiling. Dominated by C3-PARTNR, which has the stronger ablation ladder and oracle-spec kill test.

RCRS genuinely needs decentralization: I verified the shipped comm profiles, e.g. montreal comms-03-midle has one 4,000 B radio channel with input failure 0.2 and output dropout 0.1, plus voice with 0.1 dropout. But the SOTA anchor is weak. There are no published per-map scores. Timrad (2025 champion) has no code. The cloned AIT-Rescue repo's README says it is a modified PhD-thesis reproduction with bug fixes, so it is not exactly the champion binary. The official score mixes perception, pathing and fire physics, so allocation gains may be diluted. Runs are wall-clock timed and noisy (about 20-30 paired seeds per map). The Java/ADF build takes 4+ weeks. The deadline-feasibility gate is exactly the kind of mechanism that collapsed to an EDF rule in CBJA, although the prespecified EDF and Hungarian baselines are good. The CFSTP secondary uses a 2010-era random benchmark with little community traction.

Same RCRS credibility problems as LiTCo, and roughly 3 months of Java work. The levers (channel oversubscription, redundant reporting, staleness) are plausible and code-verified, but the most likely outcome is that 'newest-first + dedup + fair share 4000/N' captures most of the gain, which reviewers would call packing engineering. The claim that 'all profiles have one 4,000 B radio channel' is inaccurate: vc/comms-04-many has five 256 B radio channels. The oracle-information pilot is a good kill test. Too far from the MRTA/CBBA SOTA story.

CV_MRTA is a 2-week-old preprint with no license (written permission required), a tiny core and 0 stars, and it is near-degenerate on static instances: a replicated PyVRP wins with zero messages, which the authors concede. Their own decomposition shows MinSum collapses to 'greedy + per-robot re-sequencing' (within 2.1-3.5%), which is the CBJA trap. The MinMax headroom (1.13-1.25x at 6 robots) mixes the gain from reallocation with realized-step overhead from collision detours. The SOTA claim therefore has to rest on a self-defined dynamic, lossy extension. Prior art on post-auction exchange is dense: LNS-Auction, TraderBots, Zheng & Koenig, MGM-k. Certified 2PC commits are a useful graft but not a headline.

Verified from arXiv 2507.05178 Table 3: every LLM framework scores at or below Do-Nothing on Extinguish (-593 to -636 vs -520), Contain (-737 to -757 vs -661) and the Full Environment, and 0 on Search and Rescue. The paper used 3-10 seeds and has no non-LLM baseline. Beating the published numbers is therefore trivial and proves nothing, so the real contrast is against the authors' own ring-firebreak or distance-CBBA plus shield baselines (the self-baseline trap). The benchmark is niche (one lab, about 11 citers). The Unity 2021.3 headless build and bit-exact JAX-port parity are serious feasibility risks. A deterministic CA with an oracle-map upper bound invites the charge of simulator exploitation. The result reads as a wildfire controller, not a general group-mission allocator.

LoRR would be the most credible leaderboard, but the scheduler track has little headroom on official instances. I re-parsed the Code-Archive 2024 README: No Man's Sky's recomputed score is 6.889 (reported 6.876), and even a per-instance portfolio of all 22 scheduler entries reaches only 6.994 (+1.7%). The per-instance best scheduler ratios of 0.36-0.54 on RANDOM-03..05 are planner-limited. NMS also won 2026 Scheduling. GRAND's +10% was measured on self-generated maps of at most 500 agents with no code. The benchmark is centralized, so the decentralized and lossy axis is self-defined. It needs C++ at 10k agents in under 200 ms per tick and JAX-surrogate RL, about 14 weeks. The fluid-LP-dual collapse target is likely to match learned prices.

judgments.grafts: (1) CRITICAL CORRECTION FOR ALL HeteroMRTA CANDIDATES. The strongest published reference per configuration is min(CTAS-D, RL(s.10)), not RL. On RALTestSet the shipped env_i/results.yaml holds CTAS-D at 600 s with mean timeCost/100 = 23.67 (MIPGap about 0.52). Coalition LNS ties it at 4 s (ratio 1.000 [0.984, 1.014]) and beats it by 3.7% at 30 s (0.963 [0.948, 0.976], 40/50 wins); see /tmp/claude-0/-home-jovyan-dev-cbja/c781ca93-ceaa-4220-85a3-510892818ead/scratchpad/ac_ctasd_check.py. Reframe the claim as Pareto dominance of quality against compute across all 13 configurations: a few percent over the MILP incumbent at 20-150x less time where it solves, and 10-20% over RL where CTAS-D fails (SA-AT and MA-AT, km=50). Run the large AT configurations first, since the headline margin is decided there. Add a CP-SAT/OR-Tools time-limited reference and an OR synchronized-VRP ALNS baseline, because reviewers will ask for both. (2) Add CBTA (Wang, Liu, Qiu, Zhou, RA-L 2022, DOI 10.1109/LRA.2022.3220155; verified abstract: consensus timetable for simultaneous multi-agent tasks, beats CBGA) together with CBGA as the mandatory CBBA-lineage coalition baselines under loss. (3) Merge KOC-LNS and SyncCoal. Use KOC-LNS's simple plan-level max-consensus and replicated same-seed LNS as the zero-message ablation floor. Use SyncCoal's key-order deadlock lemma, max-plus timing CRDT, and lease-based 2PC coalition commits (the certified-commit guarantees of CERT-LNS P1-P3) as the execution layer, which becomes the novelty. (4) Make the decentralized regime non-degenerate and prespecified. Use online task reveal to the nearest robot, LoRR-2026-style Bernoulli/Poisson execution delays and partitions, and log the plan-divergence rate against replicated LNS from week 1, with a kill below 5%. (5) From DiSCo, use the H100s only for an NDS-style learned destroy selector or warm start, reported as an ablation. (6) From C3-PARTNR and LiTCo, adopt early decision-divergence logging against the best simple rule and equal-infrastructure baselines, where every method gets the same shield, channel and replay harness. (7) For a cheap second arena with exact optima, use the Sadcher 8x3 test split (CC BY 4.0) to report the gap to MILP (target well below S-Sadcher's 3.8%) and its N=20, M up to 250 scaling against Greedy. Optionally add lcpz/cfstp (MIT) to show the same coalition-LNS core generalizes to deadline-driven coalitions.

scores.rationale: Strongest SOTA odds. The pilot is real: coalition_lns_pilot.py and replay_check.py replay LNS plans in HeteroMRTA's own env. At 4 s on one core LNS scores 23.44 vs RL(s.10) 27.07, winning 50/50 instances, while construction alone scores 29.70, so the gain comes from search, not a rule. I confirmed the paper tables from the PDF text. RL(s.10) sits 15-23% above CTAS-D wherever CTAS-D solves, and takes 13-30 s at kn=50, which leaves a generous matched-time budget. Newer competitor check: BAP (RA-L Oct 2026) is a single-robot min-max multi-depot open-VRP method, not coalition, so no threat. ARMATA and the model-based RL paper (2608.21554) don't use these sets. DODRL-HMRTA is paywalled and unread. EA-ALNS (ICAACE 2026) is an unread ALNS for heterogeneous MRTA, residual risk. Risks an OR reviewer will raise: (1) Crossref confirms LNS for VRP with synchronization is established OR (Hojabri C&OR 2018; ALNS with synchronization constraints, Networks 2019), so novelty rests on decentralization. (2) On static instances plan-level max-consensus is an island model with best-plan broadcast; the decentralized layer is cosmetic, as the authors admit. (3) In SA-AT, RL is at or ahead of CTAS-D's solved subset (kn=15: 57.45 vs 58.67), so the 'every config >=5%' kill rule could trip there. (4) RALTestSet matches no paper row, so all 13 configs must be regenerated and RL reproduced against the published numbers. (5) Missing CP-SAT baseline: CP-SAT with its internal LNS at matched time is the obvious off-the-shelf OR baseline and must be beaten, not just built as an exact reference. The SOTA margin itself looks robust.

Same arena and pilot evidence as KOC-LNS: 23.53 at 4 s and 22.62 at 30 s, paired ratio 0.836 [0.825,0.847], so headroom is proven. The decentralized mechanism is richer and more defensible CBBA lineage: max-plus timing CRDT, key-ordered acyclicity, slot auctions, 2PC with leases and MGM-k arbitration. If the decentralized version keeps at least 90% of the centralized gain, the paper is stronger than KOC's. But the primary endpoint needs the distributed protocol itself to reach a ratio <=0.90 on the 4 largest configs. Getting cone-locking, lease aborts and concurrent-commit regressions right in 10 weeks is real risk, and on static instances replicated same-seed ALNS will tie it with zero messages. The flagged prior art is real: Crossref and Semantic Scholar confirm CBTA (Wang, Liu, Qiu, Zhou, RA-L 2022, 44 citations), a consensus timetable for simultaneous multi-agent tasks that beats CBGA. It is constructive, with no LNS, and must be a reimplemented baseline alongside CBGA. It shares KOC's OR-novelty problem (synchronized-VRP LNS), the SA-AT headroom uncertainty and the CP-SAT baseline gap. If the protocol underdelivers it degrades gracefully into the KOC result.

Credible external benchmark: ICLR 2025, MIT code, 1,000 paired val episodes. I verified on the HF listing that no public test split exists (train, train_132k_unverified, train_2k, train_mini, val, val_mini, ci). The oracle-spec pilot and kill criteria are well designed and separate compile error from execution error. A large efficiency win (steps, LLM calls) is likely. An SR win over a re-run frontier reasoning backbone (o3-mini already ~0.77 at small n; privileged ceiling 0.84) is uncertain. OR view: at N=2 with ~4 propositions the 'joint scheduler' is a trivial DP and almost certainly rule-equivalent (the authors admit it), so this is not an MRTA/CBBA SOTA. It is 'compiled goals + symbolic tracking beat LLM ReAct', which fits ICML/CoRL better than the stated group-mission goal. ReAct given the compiled checklist as tools may close most of the gap. Ranked third mainly to diversify away from the HeteroMRTA arena, where the top two overlap.

Same headroom evidence, but the method is dominated by its own teacher. At the HeteroMRTA matched budget (RL(s.10) takes 4-30 s per instance) the ALNS teacher run directly beats any distilled student, so the pre-registered check 'a 50 ms rolling ALNS must not match it' is likely to fail at the per-instance budget the SOTA claim uses. The learning story survives only as an ultra-low-latency or lossy-channel argument, and the latter is self-defined. A student 5-8% from the teacher lands maybe 5-10% below RL, a real margin but not the best method in the paper. 12-week timeline. Best used as the optional learned destroy operator (NDS-style) inside KOC or SyncCoal rather than as the headline.

Mechanism lever (i) is verified in code: rcrs-server RadioChannel.pushImpl adds each message to usedBandwidth and throws 'Discarding message' once over budget, first come first served. The premise is overstated, though. The 'one 4,000 B radio channel in every official profile' layout holds only for the kobe, sakae and montreal profile family. My tabulation of rcrs-scenarios shows berlin, istanbul, ny, paris and test with 3-11 channels (for example 2000+4x256 B in comms-03-mixed), and eindhoven, joao and sf with 64 B very-limited profiles. The AIT-Rescue repo (MIT) is a thesis-maintained version of the 2024 winner with bug fixes and refactors (README), not the exact competition code. Score is diluted by fire, blockade and search physics. Heavy Java/ADF engineering, 20+ paired seeds per map because of nondeterminism, a small community and no per-map published numbers. Decentralization is genuinely necessary here, which is its main merit.

I verified the CFSTP numbers in lcpz/cfstp results (CFLA2 43.76% vs EDF 32.34% vs CTS 26.37% at 4 agents; 83.59% vs 65.33% at 10). That solver-level secondary is cheap and winnable: CFLA2 is a greedy one-step lookahead, and an LNS should beat it clearly, though it is a synthetic 2010 generator. The RCRS primary shares FRESH's problems: a thesis-modified AIT codebase, allocation gains diluted by perception, pathing and fire modules, 10-min runs with high noise, no per-map scores and a small community. The deadline-gated slot bid is close to 'EDF plus coalition sizing'. The pilot's oracle-savable-deaths bound is the right first move, but I expect it to show modest headroom. Novelty is moderate given Ramchurn's CFSTP and max-sum RCRS lineage.

I verified Table 3 from the arXiv HTML. On Extinguish and Contain every LLM framework scores below Do-Nothing (-593 to -757 vs -520/-661). The Locate levels equal Do-Nothing, Search and Rescue scores 0, and runs use only 3-10 seeds. Beating the published numbers is therefore near-certain but proves little: the scientific claim rests on self-built rule baselines (ring firebreak, distance-CBBA plus shield), the CBJA self-baseline trap. The forecast-priced CBBA-TW with a learned inverse fire model is a genuinely interesting OR/ML mechanism. But the CA is deterministic given hidden Perlin fields, so an oracle planner is near-optimal and value hinges on inference quality. The Unity/Dojo build path (no prebuilt Linux binary found in the README) is a hard blocker risk. Benchmark credibility is low for MRTA reviewers.

The OR analysis is honest and correct. On MinSum, greedy insertion plus per-robot re-sequencing is within 2-3.5% of near-optimal, so inter-robot LNS matters only for MinMax at high tasks-per-robot. There a large margin over the six published allocators is likely: realized MinMax at 6 robots is 1.17-1.36x the reference. But CV_MRTA is a 2-week-old preprint with no reuse license (the critic verified license=null), and static known instances let a replicated PyVRP min-max solver dominate with zero messages. The SOTA claim must therefore move to a self-defined dynamic/private-information extension, the CBJA credibility trap. Prior art on post-auction exchange (LNS-Auction 2017, TraderBots, reaction functions, MGM-k) caps novelty. The certified 2PC commit design is sound and reusable.

Same PARTNR arena as C3-PARTNR, but less carefully scoped: no oracle-spec bound, and a weaker plan for isolating compile error. With 2 agents and a CBBA-equivalent greedy over ~4 propositions, replicated allocation is trivially rule-equivalent. Most of any SR gain will come from the goal parser, which has prior art (FLEET, AHAT/TGPO, LaMMA-P). The test split is unreleased (verified), so everything is on val. Not a group-mission MRTA SOTA. Dominated by foundation-model-era-1.

The highest-credibility arena if won: AAMAS co-hosted LoRR, where No Man's Sky won Scheduling in both 2024 and 2026 (critic verified). But evidence in the pool says scheduler-only headroom on the official instances is small. Another agent's parse of the 2024 Code-Archive finds that a per-instance portfolio of every 2024 scheduler entry reaches only 6.994 vs 6.876, and GRAND's gain shrinks from +10.7% to about 4% at 500 agents. GRAND is close prior art (learned regional guidance). The needed C++ auction at 10k agents under a 1 s tick plus a JAX surrogate plus PPO is about 14 weeks, beyond the window. The centralized metric gives decentralization no credit, and the fluid-LP-dual ablation is a likely collapse target.

judgments.grafts:
The top two share one engine (key-ordered coalition LNS on HeteroMRTA/Sadcher). Build one project: KOC-LNS as the quality core and the fallback paper, with SyncCoal's local coalition-cone commits (timing CRDT, 2PC leases, frozen execution prefix) as the decentralized execution layer. Evaluate the decentralized layer where it can matter: stochastic durations, online task arrivals, Sadcher precedence and partitions, prespecified.

OR-credibility grafts:
(1) Add CP-SAT at matched wall-clock (interval variables plus per-agent circuits, run with its internal LNS workers) as a baseline, not only as an exact reference. An OR reviewer will otherwise say the benchmark's MILP (CTAS-D, MIPGap 0.55 at 600 s) was just a weak formulation. Also report CP-SAT lower bounds, i.e. gap-to-bound on kn<=25.
(2) Regenerate all 13 HeteroMRTA configs and first reproduce the RL/Greedy numbers against the paper (RALTestSet matches no table row).
(3) Add CBTA (Wang et al. RA-L 2022, a consensus timetable for simultaneous multi-agent tasks, verified) and CBGA as the CBBA-lineage coalition baselines. Include replicated same-seed LNS and central-LNS-plus-broadcast as the collapse controls.
(4) Prespecify SA-AT as the risk family; RL is at or ahead of CTAS-D there. Relax the 'every config >=5%' kill rule to a Holm-corrected pooled endpoint plus per-family reporting.
(5) From LiTCo, add Ramchurn's CFSTP benchmark (lcpz/cfstp, MIT, 100x300-task instances, CFLA2/EDF/CTS numbers verified) as a cheap second external arena with deadlines. A coalition LNS should beat CFLA2's one-step lookahead clearly, which broadens the claim beyond one lab's test set.
(6) From DiSCo, the ALNS-teacher distillation becomes an NDS-style learned destroy selector ablation, not the headline.
(7) From FRESH, use designated-reporter and per-byte pricing to gossip plan deltas under bandwidth caps. The RCRS kernel's hard over-budget discard (verified in RadioChannel.pushImpl) is a good realistic bandwidth model for the tertiary loss study.
(8) From C3-PARTNR, the oracle-spec upper-bound pattern maps onto HeteroMRTA as a clairvoyant CP-SAT bound under stochastic durations, so decentralized-execution losses can be decomposed.

Novelty residuals to read before committing: DODRL-HMRTA (Neurocomputing 2026, paywalled) and EA-ALNS (ICAACE 2026). BAP (RA-L 2026) was checked: it is single-robot min-max open VRP, not a coalition competitor.

scores.rationale: I re-ran the pilot myself (scratchpad verify_lns_vs_ctasd.py). At 4 s on one core, Python LNS gives 23.6 against RL(s.10) 27.07 (ratio 0.873). That only TIES the RALTestSet's shipped CTAS-D 600 s Gurobi incumbent (mean 23.67; LNS/CTAS-D 1.003; wins 18/50). At 30 s it scores 22.70: 0.839 vs RL(s.10) and 0.964 vs CTAS-D (42/50 wins). The margin over the strongest learned method is therefore real and large, and it is not a rule: construction alone is worse than RL. Over the MILP incumbent it is about 4%, and it needs a compiled evaluator to be shown at matched time. Where CTAS-D fails (0-40% success) the margin over RL should hold. Balance-Aware Pointerformer (RA-L 2026, Crossref/S2 checked) is a min-max open VRP, not coalition, so it does not compete on these sets. No LNS entry turned up among HeteroMRTA's 42 S2 citers; DODRL-HMRTA's abstract was unavailable. From a field-systems view, the monotone, idempotent plan max-consensus plus frozen-prefix execution is the lowest-risk loss-tolerant design in the set. Its decentralized contribution on static instances is honestly only parallel seeds, so the CBBA-lineage claim is thin. Weak points: the benchmark is from a single lab, novelty is 'search beats one-shot RL', and the kill rule '<5% on ANY config' will likely trip on the MA-AT/SA-AT sets, where RL already beats CTAS-D. The robustness regime is self-defined unless a published delay model is used.

It uses the same verified quality gain as KOC-LNS: 30 s LNS is 0.839 vs RL(s.10) and 0.964 vs CTAS-D on RALTestSet (my re-run). The field-relevant pieces are more novel: a max-plus timing CRDT gives every robot exact coalition start times under fair-lossy links, leases bound waiting when a partner is delayed, and a global key order makes deadlock-freedom checkable by ablation. The closest CBBA-lineage prior art is CBTA (Wang et al., RA-L 2022, verified via S2), a consensus timetable for simultaneous multi-agent tasks. CBTA has no LNS and no loss model, so it makes a good extra baseline. Implementation risk is high. Two-phase commit over lossy links is blocking, commit probability falls roughly as q^(2k), and with realistic per-round latency, move throughput will be orders of magnitude below replicated centralized LNS. The prespecified 'retain at least 90% of the central gain' and '3% TOST' targets are therefore at real risk. On static instances a zero-message replicated solver dominates, so the decentralized value appears only under delays and loss, which is a partly self-defined regime. Ten weeks is tight for a correct 2PC plus MGM-k plus CRDT stack.

This is the most field-realistic arena: native radio bandwidth caps, dropout and channel failure, 30-150 heterogeneous agents, partial observability and hard deadlines. AIT-Rescue is MIT-licensed and claims the 2024 title (repo checked). I verified the CFSTP numbers in lcpz/cfstp results (CFLA2 43.8 / 74.3 / 83.6% vs EDF 32.3 / 57.2 / 65.3% at 4 / 8 / 10 agents). Risks: (1) the official score blends search, pathing, fire physics and allocation, so allocation gains may be diluted to a few points; (2) wall-clock-timed simulations are nondeterministic and need 20-30 seeds per map; (3) Java ADF engineering takes 4+ weeks; (4) no per-map published scores exist and the 2025 champion's code is unavailable, and the rescuesim site shows no 2024-2026 results page. CFSTP SOTA also has to contend with CCF's claim of up to 10% over CFLA2. The gain may reduce to EDF plus a coalition-size rule. The pilot's oracle clairvoyant-CFSTP bound is the right kill test. For AAMAS it is credible if it wins, but ICRA and NeurIPS reviewers discount RCRS.

The arena is the weakest. CV_MRTA still has no license and 0 stars (README re-checked 2026-09-27), is a two-week-old preprint, and its static instances are near-degenerate: ideal-link planners already sit near the bound, and a replicated PyVRP needs zero messages. The candidate admits the SOTA claim must come from a self-defined dynamic, private-discovery, lossy variant, which is the CBJA credibility trap. Headroom at 6 robots x 50-100 targets (1.29-1.36x reference) is real but vanishes at 16 robots, and on MinSum a trivial re-sequencing rule is within 2-3.5%. The version-checked 2PC with leases (at most one owner under any loss) is sound field engineering. Post-auction exchange is old prior art, though: LNS-Auction, TraderBots, Zheng and Koenig, MGM-k. The work also needs written permission from the authors. There is a scoop risk from the GACA group's loss-mechanism work.

It targets the same HeteroMRTA arena, but my re-run shows the teacher, not the student, is the SOTA engine. A 4 s single-core ALNS already equals CTAS-D and beats RL(s.10) by 13%, so at the matched 4 s budget a distilled student can only lose to its own teacher. The claim therefore survives only at a 20-50 ms per-decision budget, where a rolling-horizon ALNS is the natural competitor (the candidate's own kill check). Reviewers will ask why the robot does not just run ALNS on board, since it is CPU-cheap. DAgger under lossy channels with teammate-claim prediction is a genuinely field-relevant idea: robots act on stale state. But it rests on a self-defined loss extension, and it takes 12 weeks of GPU-heavy work, which exceeds the budget. There is a scoop risk because SADCHER's stated future work is exactly this.

I parsed the LoRR 2024 Code-Archive README. A per-instance portfolio of all 22 Scheduler-track entries is only about 1.8% above No Man's Sky, which also won Scheduling in 2026. Scheduler headroom on the official instances with the default planner is therefore tiny, and those instances are planner- and congestion-limited. GRAND's +10% came on self-generated 200-500-agent maps and has no code, so a win there rests on a disputed reimplementation. The benchmark is centralized, so decentralization and comm loss add nothing to the metric; the loss axis is self-defined. Building a C++ auction at 10k agents within 1 s per tick, plus JAX-surrogate RL, is about 14 weeks, beyond the budget. Fluid-LP duals may match learned prices (collapse). An official-instance win would be highly credible, but it is unlikely.

This is best aligned with comm-loss realism. The lever is concrete: one shared 4,000 B radio channel for 30-150 agents, where the kernel discards overflow first-come-first-served, and per-agent budgeting in AIT oversubscribes it. The design responds sensibly: team shadow price, designated reporters, digest-driven anti-entropy and store-carry-forward under the jammer and voice-only profiles. It also uses System-1 only as tiny hazard models, which is honest. The oracle-information pilot is a good kill test. Risks: (1) under fullJammer or noneChannel only 30 m voice remains, so the attainable information gain is bounded; (2) under full or high profiles the score may be limited by fire physics and blockades, not information; (3) reviewers may call packing and deduplication 'engineering', although the prespecified newest-first+dedup and fair-share rules address that; (4) it needs about 6 weeks of Java; (5) wall-clock nondeterminism. RCRS has a small community, no per-map published numbers and no Timrad code, so the SOTA claim is 'beats the 2024 champion', which is modest outside AAMAS.

PARTNR is a credible benchmark: ICLR 2025, 1,000 val episodes, MIT code. But as an MRTA or group-mission claim it is weak: 2 agents, no channel, no loss, no asynchrony. Replicated deterministic allocation over about 4 propositions will almost surely be rule-equivalent, and most SR gain will come from the goal parser. That makes this 'compile the grader format' and not coordination. The test split is hidden, so everything must be re-run on val. Among PARTNR citers (S2), TaskGround and RoboGraph (arXiv 2608.08036) do structured task compilation for single agents, and FLEET does LLM to task graph to MILP, so novelty is thin. A re-run frontier reasoning ReAct (o3-mini already about 0.77) may narrow the SR margin. Habitat setup risk. It is a weaker version of C3-PARTNR, with no oracle-spec pilot and a vaguer tracker.

This is the best-designed of the two PARTNR candidates. It has an oracle-spec upper-bound pilot that separates compile error from execution error, an honest admission that the allocator will likely be rule-equivalent, and a ReAct-plus-compiled-tools equal-infrastructure baseline. The efficiency win (steps -35 to -55%, LLM calls -90%) is very likely. A clear SR win of +5 or more against a re-run frontier open reasoning backbone is uncertain. With n=1000 paired episodes the statistics are strong. From a multi-robot field-systems view it has little relevance: 2 agents, no comm model, and silent common-knowledge scheduling at N=2 is thin as a multi-agent contribution. MRTA and AAMAS reviewers may not count it as group-mission SOTA, while ICML and CoRL reviewers may. There is prior art in single-agent compile-then-execute (AHAT/TGPO, TaskGround, RoboGraph) and centralized FLEET. Evaluation is on val only, the labeler-learning critique is likely, and the Habitat and oracle-skill failure ceilings apply.

The idea is interesting: learned hidden-field inference plus forecast-priced CBBA with time windows and coalitions, which is realistic for wildfire missions. But beating the published numbers proves little, since the LLM frameworks score below Do-Nothing. The scientific claim rests on self-implemented ring, distance-CBBA and shield baselines, which is the CBJA self-baseline trap. I verified that Khan et al. (IEEE Access 2026, S2 abstract) report a hybrid LangGraph-CrewAI reaching '96.1% success' across all 17 CREW-Wildfire levels (3 seeds). That muddies the 'every published framework is at or below Do-Nothing' framing and must be reconciled with the official score. The biggest risk is implementation: no prebuilt headless binary (the repo points to a Unity package plus Python), so building Unity 2021.3 and Dojo may cost weeks, and the reported numbers must come from the official build. The benchmark comes from one lab with few citers. Comms are lossless broadcast, so the decentralized and loss angle is absent. A deterministic CA also invites 'simulator exploitation' critiques.

judgments.grafts: Merge benchmark-first-1 and mechanism-first-1 into one project. Use KOC-LNS's monotone, idempotent plan max-consensus plus frozen-prefix freeze as the loss-tolerant core; it is low-risk and needs no blocking protocol. Add three pieces from SyncCoal: (a) the max-plus timing CRDT so every coalition member knows the exact start time under delays; (b) lease-based reinsertion when a partner misses its lease, which bounds waiting under execution noise; (c) the no-order-layer ablation that shows deadlocks, so the key order is a necessary mechanism rather than decoration. Keep 2PC only as an optional ablation, since its throughput under loss is the main failure risk. The paper must beat CTAS-D, not just RL. My re-run showed 4 s Python LNS only ties the shipped CTAS-D 600 s incumbent (1.003, 18/50 wins), while 30 s gives 0.964 vs CTAS-D (42/50) and 0.839 vs RL(s.10). Build a numba or C++ forward-pass evaluator in week 1 so the 30 s quality is reached at RL's 4 s budget, and add a CP-SAT exact reference plus lower bounds, because CTAS-D's MIPGap is 0.3-0.65. Add CBTA (Wang et al., RA-L 2022; simultaneous multi-agent tasks, consensus timetable) and a reimplemented CBGA as the CBBA-lineage decentralized baselines, alongside 'central LNS + broadcast + local fallback' and 'replicated same-seed LNS'. For the robustness regime, use the published LoRR-2026 per-tick Bernoulli/Poisson delay model and the CV_MRTA channel models (Bernoulli, Gilbert-Elliott, Rayleigh), not self-invented ones. Also give HeteroMRTA RL stale observations under identical channel infrastructure. From DiSCo, take only the NDS-style learned destroy selector as an ablation, plus RL-with-stale-state as a baseline; do not build a distillation story. From CERT-LNS, take (a) decision-divergence logging against the replicated solver from day 1, which is the kill test for the decentralization section, and (b) the fair-lossy convergence statement for the gossip layer. From C3-PARTNR, take the oracle-spec idea as a pilot pattern (run the planner with clairvoyant delays to bound what re-planning under noise can recover). For the RCRS pair: if RCRS is kept as an external-validity arena, run LiTCo's deadline-gated coalition slots together with FRESH's team shadow-price channel arbitration and designated reporters in one ADF module. They share the arena, the AIT baseline and the oracle pilots (clairvoyant CFSTP bound plus shared-WorldInfo bound), and together they cover both the allocation lever and the information lever that decide the degraded-profile score. FRESH's bandwidth pricing can also cap the plan-gossip rate of the coalition-LNS project under a byte budget, so bytes per robot become a reported endpoint. Verification used Crossref, the Semantic Scholar API, WebFetch and local re-runs; the verification script is /tmp/claude-0/-home-jovyan-dev-cbja/c781ca93-ceaa-4220-85a3-510892818ead/scratchpad/verify_lns_vs_ctasd.py.

prior_work_found.title: HeteroMRTA: Heterogeneous Multi-robot Task Allocation and Scheduling via RL (Dai et al., RA-L 10(3) 2025) and its CTAS-D MILP baseline
prior_work_found.overlap: The paper's own MILP baseline, CTAS-D (Gurobi, 600 s), already beats RL(s.10) by about 13%. The shipped RALTestSet results.yaml gives CTAS-D 23.67 vs our RL(s.10) re-run 27.07, a ratio of 0.873. The candidate's headline '-13.4% vs published RL SOTA' is therefore the known RL-to-MILP gap, not a new result. The paper also describes its flashforward mechanism as 'search[ing] for a suitable permutation' of decisions to avoid deadlock.

prior_work_found.title: Decentralized Task Allocation in Multi-Agent Systems Using a Decentralized Genetic Algorithm (DGA; Patel et al., ICRA 2020)
prior_work_found.overlap: The abstract (read via Semantic Scholar) says DGA 'parallelizes a genetic algorithm across the team' and agents 'continuously search for and share better solutions during task execution'. That is the plan-level max-consensus parallel anytime solver, with a GA in place of LNS. DGA is also a named baseline on CV_MRTA.

prior_work_found.title: Heterogeneous Task Allocation and Sequencing via Decentralized Large Neighborhood Search (LNS-Auction; Sadeghi & Smith, Unmanned Systems 2017)
prior_work_found.overlap: Decentralized LNS for heterogeneous multi-robot allocation (destroy on the own path, repair by auction). It has no coalitions or synchronization, so KOC-LNS differs mainly by handling coalition sync.

prior_work_found.title: Ant Colony Optimization for Heterogeneous Coalition Formation and Scheduling with Multi-Skilled Robots (Babincsak, Aswale, Pinciroli, MRS 2023)
prior_work_found.overlap: An iterative metaheuristic for exactly this dynamic-coalition scheduling problem; its methods are the SAS/TACO baselines in HeteroMRTA. This undercuts the claim that the prior best methods are 'one-pass constructive': iterative search was already tried, just weakly engineered.

prior_work_found.title: Heterogeneous Coalition Formation and Scheduling with Multi-Skilled Robots (Aswale & Pinciroli, IROS 2023)
prior_work_found.overlap: Presents an optimal MILP and a fast heuristic for dynamic coalitions. Sadcher's MILP extends this formulation, so the Sadcher optima come from it.
