fatal_issues: The headline margin is misattributed. RALTestSet is the only set the pilot ran on. On it, HeteroMRTA's own shipped CTAS-D results (HeteroMRTA/RALTestSet/env_*/results.yaml) average 23.67 vs RL(s.10) 27.07, already -12.7%. Re-running the candidate's scripts (ac_ctasd_check.py) gives LNS@4s / CTAS-D = 1.002 [0.988, 1.015] with 22/50 wins, and LNS@30s / CTAS-D = 0.961 [0.948, 0.973] with 43/50 wins. Against the strongest published baseline with code, the real small-instance margin is 0-4%, not 13%. 'Matches the MILP level' also has no optimality anchor: all 50 CTAS-D runs hit the 600 s limit (optStatus 9), with mean MIP gap 52% and mean bound 11.25 against incumbents of 23.67.

The candidate's own prespecified kill criterion is already tripped, and in the regime that matters. I regenerated the published MA-AT configuration kn=25/km=50 (the MILP solves 0% there) with the repo generator; the generator validates (RL(s.10) 45.75 vs 46.98 published). The pilot LNS at matched wall-clock (18 s vs RL(s.10) 17.9 s) scores 45.67: ratio 0.998 [0.985, 1.011], 23/50 wins, i.e. a tie. The margin collapses exactly where RL is the SOTA and where the paper has to win. Only at 5x the budget (90 s) does it reach 0.936 [0.924, 0.948] with 48/50 wins, because the Python pilot runs about 56 LNS iterations/s at 50 tasks. The 'no scaling wall' claim is therefore unproven.

The decentralized, CBBA-lineage contribution is empty on the chosen arena. The instances are static, fully known and assume global communication. On MA-AT kn=15/km=20, best-of-8 seeds at 5 s scores 28.60, worse than a single seed given 40 s (28.10). Plan max-consensus is just parallel CPU, and a central server with 8 cores reproduces it. Any decentralization win would come only from the self-defined tertiary arena (Gilbert-Elliott loss on HeteroMRTA instances, with reimplemented CBGA and LNS-Auction). That is the exact CBJA failure mode, and plan sharing during execution is already DGA (ICRA 2020).
fixable_issues: Benchmark anchoring. RALTestSet (planner_param path 'RALTestSet1_3A5S20T_BT_BA': 5 species x 3 multi-skill binary agents, 20 binary tasks) matches no published table row, and the paper's test sets are not shipped. All 13 configurations must be regenerated, and RL and CTAS-D re-run (CTAS-D needs a Gurobi licence). Published CTAS-D means cover solved instances only, which is a selection bias. The generator reproduces the paper where I checked: MA-AT 15/20 gives RL(s.10) 35.28 vs 35.91 published and RL(g.) 38.68 vs 38.50 (scratchpad/rt_maat_15_20). Reproduce every configuration's RL row within CI before comparing.

The pilot evaluator drifts from the environment on additive tasks. Forward pass and env replay differ on 1/50 instances (MA-AT 15/20) and 9-11/50 (MA-AT 25/50), by up to 1.2 time units; on binary-task RALTestSet the drift was 0. Score every result by env replay and fix the evaluator semantics so the LNS optimizes the true objective.

The RL baseline is not yet fair. RL(s.10) here means 10 sequential single-thread CPU rollouts. At matched wall-clock, reviewers will require GPU-batched POMO-style sampling (s.64-s.256): already RL(g.) to RL(s.10) is -6.4% at 25/50. Also add RL(s.N) followed by the same LNS polish, CTAS-D at matched 5-60 s budgets, and a CP-SAT or CP-Optimizer interval model. Expect these to narrow the margin at 50 or more tasks.

Scale engineering. The pilot's insertion re-simulates O(T*A) per slot and fully re-evaluates each candidate, giving about 56 it/s at 50 tasks and 25 agents. Table IV scales (200-500 tasks, 50-150 agents; RL(s.10) takes 75-560 s there) need a compiled, incremental evaluator at least 10x faster. Also, wall-clock budgets shift under CPU contention (seed 0 at 5 s scored 29.83 with 90 concurrent processes vs 29.32 with 50), so use CPU-time or iteration budgets on isolated cores.

HeteroMRTA's Greedy baseline is buggy. In env/task_env.py execute_greedy_action, `dist` is never updated inside the loop, so it picks the last feasible task index rather than the nearest task. Do not present its numbers (32.7 / 45.1) as a greedy baseline; implement a correct nearest-task greedy and Sadcher's greedy.

Sadcher arena weaknesses. The 250K set is training data and the 500 test instances are generated at runtime (SEED=1). The scaling results are figure-level relative gaps over 100 runs, with no numeric table. On 8x3 instances the MILP is exact (76 s mean), so a 0-1% gap will be read as 'use the MILP'. The pilot lacks precedence and separate start/end depots. Checkpoint paths are hard-coded to the author's machine (the IL checkpoints ship; RL does not), and the code has no licence.

Novelty framing. Key order plus forward pass is the RCPSP activity-list/serial-SGS technique. LNS for synchronized multi-vehicle routing is standard (Drexl 2012; Networks 2019). ACO for this exact problem exists (MRS 2023). Position the paper as an empirical SOTA / strong-baseline result with ablations of the waiting-aware and critical-path operators, not as a new algorithmic principle.

Consensus theory trap. Max-consensus needs a common total order on plans. Once realized durations and frozen prefixes differ between robots or partitions, a plan's objective depends on each robot's beliefs, and merging under 'union of frozen prefixes' needs a repair step that breaks monotonicity and idempotence. Either put a version-stamped shared state first in the order key or drop the convergence claim for the execution phase.

prior_work_found.title: SADCHER (Bichler et al., MRS 2025)
prior_work_found.overlap: No metaheuristic, local-search or CP baseline. The MILP averages 76 s on 8 tasks x 3 robots. Beating S-Sadcher's 3.8% gap at that size with any search method is expected, not a SOTA signal. Code has no license.

fatal_issues: The headline margin is against the wrong baseline. On the named arena, CTAS-D (published, code in the repo, results shipped in RALTestSet) already beats RL(s.10) by 13-18% on every SA-BT set it solves. My paired runs on the 50 shipped instances: pilot LNS at 4 s vs CTAS-D at 600 s = 0.998 [0.982, 1.012], a tie. At 30 s = 0.959 [0.945, 0.971], only 4.1% better. The claimed '12-16% below the strongest published method with code' does not hold; the real margin over the strongest published method is 0-4% on this set. On SA-BT kn=50/km=50, one of the four configurations in the primary endpoint, CTAS-D is at 0.815 x RL. The pre-registered success level (SyncCoal/RL <= 0.90) would still lose to CTAS-D there by about 9%.

A stock solver reproduces the margin. Untuned OR-Tools CP-SAT, from a model written in about 15 minutes with no hints, matches the pilot LNS at equal wall-clock on RALTestSet: 0.868 x RL at 4 s and 0.834 at 30 s on 8 threads, vs LNS 0.868 and 0.836. Plans were replayed in HeteroMRTA's simulator with zero discrepancy. On the shipped set the SOTA margin therefore belongs to 'use any competent combinatorial solver', not to SyncCoal.

The CBJA failure mode returns in a new form: the novel mechanism does nothing measurable on the primary endpoint. The instances are static and fully known, so a replicated centralized LNS or CP-SAT run with a shared seed produces the same plan with zero messages. The max-plus CRDT, consensus order keys, 2PC and MGM-k can at best tie the centralized optimizer; the pre-registered TOST vs centralized ALNS says exactly that. The only regime where decentralization could add value (execution delays plus message loss) is self-defined on this benchmark. HeteroMRTA assumes global communication, and the LoRR 2026 delay model comes from grid MAPF execution. The natural strong baselines in that regime are missing from the list: a replicated solver plus event gossip, and a central re-solve plus broadcast plus local fallback (CBJA's own lesson).

The parallelism premise behind 'decentralized keeps the gain' is false at benchmark scale. In good plans (CP-SAT at 30 s, RALTestSet), a single-task change reaches a mean 42% of robots through the synchronization DAG. A typical q-task ruin reaches a median 73% (mean 69%), and 75% of moves touch at least half the team (coalition size 2.6, 3.5 tasks per robot). Concurrent proposals therefore almost always overlap in write set or timing cone, so MGM-k locking plus 2PC serializes the search. The result is a centralized LNS with multi-party commit latency, not about N-fold throughput. Under p=0.5 loss, every commit needs prepare/ack/commit among about 10 robots, which is expected to cut the commit rate drastically. Retaining 90% of the centralized gain at equal wall-clock is not credible.

Stated guarantee Q3 (coalition atomicity) cannot be achieved over lossy links in bounded time (Two Generals / atomic commitment). 2PC with leases gives bounded waiting and later reinsertion, not atomicity: if the commit message to a prepared participant is lost, the lease expires and one robot travels while another does not. Q1 is folklore: every deadlock-free synchronized schedule is sortable by start time, and Bischoff et al. 2020 give the feasibility criterion. Q2 is redundant, because robots holding a replicated plan compute max-plus start times locally. The theory contribution will not survive review as stated.
fixable_issues: The primary endpoint (ratio to RL(s.10) over the 4 largest configurations) is chosen where CTAS-D mostly fails. Include CTAS-D where it succeeds (SA-BT 50/50: 18.65 at 3600 s), CP-SAT, and RL with more samples on GPU at equal wall-clock (RL(s.10) ran single-thread on CPU in the pilot).

At scale the centralized margin is real but must be attributed to LNS. On 30 fresh 50-agent x 50-task instances (repo generator, seeds 5000-5029), RL(s.10) scores 18.56 at 12.8 s. Pilot LNS: 16.05 at 13 s (0.860 [0.837, 0.883]) and 15.66 at 30 s (0.840 [0.813, 0.865]), better on 30/30. Naive CP-SAT finds nothing in 30 s. A reframed 'coalition ALNS at scale' claim is plausible, but it is an OR-technique result, not a CBBA-lineage one.

Implementation trap: the pilot evaluator's exact match with the simulator holds only on the SA-BT RALTestSet. On multi-skill 50x50 instances, replay differs from the evaluator by up to 0.48 per instance (mean +0.016), presumably from early starts when the coalition includes redundant members. Every reported number must come from env replay.

Sadcher secondary: beating a 3.8% gap on 8 tasks x 3 robots is expected of any search method (MILP takes 76 s on average). Use the scaling protocol (20 robots, more than 70 tasks, where Greedy beats S-Sadcher) and add CP-SAT/MILP with time limits. The code has no license, so run it unmodified.

Missing baselines reviewers will require: CBTA (RA-L 2022), coupled-constraint CBBA, CBGA, ITAGS/Q-ITAGS, a synchronized-VRP ALNS reimplementation, warm-started and tuned CP-SAT, replicated solver plus gossip, and central re-solve plus local fallback.

Benchmark credibility is moderate: single-lab sets, 42 citations, no third-party leaderboard, only 50 shipped instances, and SAS/TACO replays that do not match the paper (29.74 vs 27.41; 38.92 vs 35.07). Regenerate all 12 configurations with released seeds, and state that the generator's defaults are multi-skill.

redteam.minimal_change_to_survive:
Drop the decentralized-SOTA framing and the claim of 12-16% over the strongest published method. Two changes are needed.

(1) Make the SOTA claim an anytime coalition ruin-and-recreate optimizer (centralized or replicated, parallel on 96 cores), evaluated where exact and CP methods fail: the regenerated SA-AT and MA-AT 50/50 sets and the Table IV sets (50x200, 150x500). Evaluate at equal wall-clock and hardware against the full set: CTAS-D at its time limit, warm-started and tuned CP-SAT, RL(s.N) on GPU, Greedy, S-Sadcher at 20 robots with more than 70 tasks, ITAGS-style search, and CBTA. Pre-register a kill: fewer than 8% below the best of these on the large configurations means no paper. On the shipped 15x20 set, report the tie with CP-SAT and the 4% over CTAS-D honestly.

(2) Shrink the decentralized part to what holds: a replicated plan, deterministic merge of gossiped execution events (a CRDT), consensus order keys for deadlock-freedom, and bounded-wait reinsertion. Drop 2PC/MGM-k parallel LNS and the atomicity claim. Evaluate it only in a regime where information is private or dynamic, against a replicated solver plus gossip and a central re-solve plus local fallback. Better still, move that claim to an arena with native decentralized coalition baselines, such as CFSTP/D-CTS (London Fire Brigade data, MIT code).

Even reframed, the likely outcome is a solid RA-L 'search beats learned MRTA at scale' paper, not a CBBA-lineage decentralized SOTA.

fatal_issues: The candidate replaces the fixed human partner, so it breaks the official protocol. In PARTNR's automated evaluation the humanoid is always the zero-shot ReAct Llama-3.1-70B, and only the robot planner changes. Evidence: paper §4.2.1 ('we also need a simulated human partner, which we control with a ReAct approach, using Llama3.1-70B-Instruct'). §A.9: for the finetuned robot, 'simulation time and human agent inference time remained unchanged'. Table 10: 'ReAct-8B uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the robot model'. Code: decentralized_ft_human_react_summary.yaml overrides only agent_0. C3's central mechanism runs the same deterministic joint scheduler on both agents, so the humanoid would run C3. That is not the protocol behind the Finetuned, ReAct-8B or RAG rows, and it contradicts the benchmark's human-robot premise (HITL). Under the faithful protocol (C3 robot, ReAct-70B human) the partner does not run the scheduler, so silent common-knowledge coordination cannot work.

Where both agents are controlled, the replicated scheduler is centralized planning computed twice. Both copies run one deterministic program on common-knowledge inputs. The fair comparators are then centralized ReAct with partial observability (0.74 SR / 2,298 steps) and the Heuristic-Expert run on the compiled spec, not decentralized ReAct at 3,295 steps. Against those, the projected margin (about 0.74-0.80 SR, about 2,000 steps) shrinks to 0-6 SR points and about 13% fewer steps.

Coordination does not move SR on PARTNR, so any SR gain is a single-agent parsing and tracking gain, not a multi-agent one. Val SR is flat across control modes: single 0.73, decentralized 0.73, centralized 0.74, and decentralized with full observability 0.74. Per task type (Table 13) it is also flat: decentralized 0.82/0.82/0.60/0.66 vs centralized 0.84/0.85/0.59/0.66 vs single 0.85/0.81/0.58/0.68. The candidate itself concedes the allocator will be rule-equivalent at N=2 with about 4 propositions. The result could at best be a neurosymbolic instruction-following SOTA on a 2-agent household benchmark. It would not be the decentralized group-mission or task-allocation algorithm SOTA the researcher wants. This repeats the CBJA lesson that the architecture, not the allocator, carries the effect.
